problem_statement:
## Description
In the CV32A65X configuration of CVA6, the RISC-V machine interrupt CSRs expose the machine software interrupt bits even though the specification says these bits are not implemented for this single-hart system. Specifically, bit 3 of `mip` (`MSIP`, machine software interrupt pending) and bit 3 of `mie` (`MSIE`, machine software interrupt enable) should be fixed to zero.

## Expected Behavior
For CV32A65X, reads of `mip.MSIP` and `mie.MSIE` must always return `0`. Writing `mie` with `MSIE=1` must not make that bit read back as `1`, and `mip.MSIP` must remain `0` rather than becoming visible as pending state.

## Actual Behavior
The RTL allows the machine software interrupt bits to become visible instead of remaining hardwired to zero. As a result, software can observe `mie.MSIE=1` after writing `mie`, and `mip.MSIP` can appear set in a configuration where both bits should be read-only zero.

## Affected Function
This affects the CSR logic that implements the RISC-V machine interrupt enable and pending registers (`mie` and `mip`) for the CV32A65X configuration.

## Trigger Condition
The bug appears when software reads or writes the machine software interrupt bits in CV32A65X, especially when writing `mie` with bit 3 set or when observing the pending software-interrupt state in `mip`.

problem_statement:
## Description
In RV32 (32-bit RISC-V) configurations of CVA6, the instruction decoder incorrectly accepts reserved encodings of the RISC-V bit-manipulation immediate instructions `BCLRI`, `BINVI`, `BSETI`, `BEXTI`, and `RORI`. For these five instructions, instruction bit 25 is reserved in RV32 and must be zero.

## Expected Behavior
When CVA6 decodes any of these instructions in RV32, the encoding with bit 25 cleared must be treated as legal, and the encoding with bit 25 set must be rejected by raising an illegal instruction exception.

## Actual Behavior
CVA6 currently decodes these instructions as legal in RV32 even when bit 25 is set, so no illegal instruction exception is raised for the reserved encoding.

## Affected Function
Instruction decode logic for RV32 bit-manipulation immediate instructions, specifically the path that classifies `BCLRI`, `BINVI`, `BSETI`, `BEXTI`, and `RORI` and decides whether to raise an illegal instruction exception.

## Trigger Condition
The bug is triggered when an RV32 CVA6 core decodes `BCLRI`, `BINVI`, `BSETI`, `BEXTI`, or `RORI` with instruction bit 25 equal to 1.

resolved_issues.title: mmu: Latch misaligned exception to fix misattribution
resolved_issues.body:
The load and store units sample the MMU exception one cycle after `dtlb_hit` is asserted (see below). However, misaligned exceptions are currently fed through the MMU, potentially attributing a misaligned exception to the *preceding* instruction. Fix this by latching the misaligned exception.

https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/6e0cf8d7307f8e7b1aa4d9b09d1cd5254426de0a/core/load_unit.sv#L436-L442

problem_statement:
## Description
CVA6's memory management unit (MMU) reports load/store misaligned exceptions on a one-cycle-delayed interface to the load/store unit (LSU). The LSU consumes the MMU response one cycle after the request phase, but the misaligned-exception state is not kept with the originating request across that delay. As a result, the exception seen with an LSU response can come from the wrong request cycle instead of the memory access that actually faulted.

## Expected Behavior
For RISC-V load and store address-misaligned faults, the exception reported by the MMU-to-LSU response path must belong to the same memory access that caused it. A response for a misaligned access should appear on the following LSU response cycle with the correct misaligned exception, and a cycle with no pending LSU response must not expose a leftover misaligned exception.

## Actual Behavior
The MMU can present a misaligned exception from the wrong cycle. This can misattribute the exception to a different load/store response, and in the boundary case where the original misaligned access is followed by a cycle with no LSU request, a stale misaligned exception can still remain visible.

## Affected Function
The MMU-to-LSU load/store response path for misaligned-access exception reporting.

## Trigger Condition
This occurs when a misaligned load or store enters the MMU and the corresponding LSU response is consumed one cycle later. If the next cycle does not match the original request context, especially when there is no new LSU request, the misaligned exception can be reported on the wrong cycle or leak into the idle cycle.

resolved_issues.title: [BUG] mtinst corrupted
resolved_issues.body:
### Is there an existing CVA6 bug for this?

- [x] I have searched the existing bug issues

### Bug Description

Hello,
I have noticed an unexpected behavior.
The signal x_exception_o in cvxif_fu has several unconnected fields, which is partially intentional (at least for tval) according to the specification.
In certain scenarios, and with the hypervisor extension enabled, it is possible that these undriven fields are read and the CSR mtinst is written with these arbitrary values.
I have created a small test bench here: https://github.com/KatCe/cva6/tree/bug_mtinst_corruption/bug_simulations/x_exception_mtinst
In this test bench, the bug is triggered by an unexpected bus response that also triggers an assertion:

	** Fatal: Trying to pop data although the FIFO is empty.
	#    Time: 25 ns Started: 25 ns  Scope: tb_top.i_ariane.gen_cache_wt.i_cache_subsystem.i_adapter.i_rd_icache_id.empty_read File:../core/cva6_fifo_v3.sv Line: 228

To model what would happen in silicon I have initialized the tinst field of x_exception_o with an arbitrary value for demonstration (https://github.com/KatCe/cva6/blob/bug_mtinst_corruption/core/cvxif_fu.sv#66) and converted the assertion to a warning (https://github.com/KatCe/cva6/blob/bug_mtinst_corruption/core/cva6_fifo_v3.sv#228).
In that case we see the arbitrary value written to the mtinst CSR.

While this exact scenario can only happen if cva6 is integrated with another component that does not follow the bus protocol, I believe that cva6 should not rely on a bug free external world. Furthermore, a fault injection attack could trigger this CSR corruption.

I have not yet investigated whether this corruption can also be triggered by other scenarios.

problem_statement:
## Description
CVA6 reports illegal-instruction exceptions from its CVXIF custom-instruction interface through the `x_exception_o` record produced by `cvxif_fu`. When the RISC-V hypervisor extension (RVH) is enabled, the illegal-instruction path does not fully initialize the hypervisor-specific fields of that record. Trap handling can then consume undefined metadata, and `mtinst` (the machine-trap transformed-instruction CSR) may capture arbitrary values instead of deterministic exception state.

## Expected Behavior
For a CVXIF-generated illegal-instruction exception, the exception record must be fully defined before trap CSRs consume it. The cause must remain illegal instruction, the rejected instruction value in `tval` must stay correct when that field is enabled, hypervisor-only payload fields that have no meaningful value on this path must be zero, and the guest-virtual-address flag must match the current virtualization state rather than an undefined or stale value.

## Actual Behavior
With RVH enabled, the illegal-instruction path can leave hypervisor-specific metadata in `x_exception_o` undriven. This makes transformed-instruction metadata non-deterministic and can corrupt `mtinst`; other hypervisor exception fields may also depend on arbitrary logic state.

## Affected Function
The CVXIF exception-generation logic in `cvxif_fu`, specifically the illegal-instruction exception record emitted on `x_exception_o`.

## Trigger Condition
The bug is triggered when the CVXIF functional unit rejects an instruction and raises an illegal-instruction exception while CVA6 is built with the hypervisor extension enabled.

problem_statement:
## Description
CVA6 has separate instruction and data translation lookaside buffers (ITLB and DTLB). In the MMU, the DTLB lookup uses the instruction-side address-space identifier (ASID) instead of the ASID for the current load/store translation context. As a result, the DTLB can search with the wrong ASID when instruction fetch and load/store translation are in different virtualization contexts.

## Expected Behavior
A DTLB lookup must be keyed by the ASID of the load/store request being translated. After a guest load fills a DTLB entry for a virtual address under a given guest ASID, a later guest load to the same virtual address under that same guest ASID must hit the cached DTLB entry and must not start a new page-table walk.

## Actual Behavior
When the load/store path and instruction path use different ASIDs, the DTLB lookup uses the instruction-side ASID. The entry created for the guest load is then not matched on the next lookup, so the repeated guest load misses in the DTLB and triggers another page-table walk even though the translation was already cached.

## Affected Functionality
This affects the CVA6 MMU data-translation path, specifically ASID-qualified DTLB lookup and tag matching for guest or virtualized memory accesses.

## Trigger Condition
The problem becomes visible when the RISC-V H extension is enabled and the ASID used for load/store translation differs from the ASID used by instruction fetch, for example when a guest data access uses a guest ASID while instruction fetch remains in the host context. It is usually masked when the H extension is disabled because the instruction-side and data-side lookup ASIDs are the same in that case.

title: Fix cvxif_off_instr_n in issue_read_operands
body:
Currently, cvxif_off_instr_n is assigned to orig_instr[i], with i being 0 or 1 depending on the issue port.

This assigns the original instruction value (which will be propagated, e.g., into tval in an exception) to the last bit of the instruction on issue port 0.

This commit assigns it to the full instruction on the corresponding issue port instead.

Fixes https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/issues/2935.

resolved_issues.title: [BUG] Incorrect assignment of original instruction in issue_read_operands?
resolved_issues.body:
### Is there an existing CVA6 bug for this?

- [x] I have searched the existing bug issues

### Bug Description

Some traps on floating point instructions when the FPU is disabled convey an incorrect *tval*.
For example, on traps in machine mode, I have had an mtval of `1` instead of the actual instruction `0x2b007`.

I have traced the issue back to `issue_read_operands.sv`.
Consider this assignment: https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/30811d1e7e3977b557190e7fa3d5753844cf9591/core/issue_read_operands.sv#L883
I believe you want to assign to `orig_instr_i[i]` here instead, as `orig_instr` is always assigned to `orig_instr_i[0]`.
The statement currently appears to extract only one bit of the instruction, which would explain the mtval of `1`.

Changing the assignment accordingly has fixed the problem I have seen. I am happy to send a PR with this change if you agree this is the correct solution.

      version="$(sed -n 's@.*verilator-\([0-9][0-9.]*\)\.t.*@\1@p' "$script" | head -n1)"
    fi
  fi
  echo "$version"
}

preinstalled_verilator_dir() {
  case "$1" in
    v5.008|v5.018)
      echo "/tools/verilator-$1"
      ;;
    *)
      return 1
      ;;
  esac
}

fix_verilator_layout() {
  local prefix="$1"
  if [[ -d "$prefix/share/verilator/include" ]]; then
    ln -sfn "$prefix/share/verilator/include" "$prefix/include"
  fi
  if [[ -x "$prefix/share/verilator/bin/verilator_includer" ]]; then
    ln -sfn "$prefix/share/verilator/bin/verilator_includer" "$prefix/bin/verilator_includer"
  fi
}

build_verilator_on_demand() {
  local script="$1"
  local version="$2"
  local prefix="$3"
  if [[ "$script" == "verif/regress/install-verilator.sh" ]]; then
    echo "[INFO] Building Verilator via $script into $prefix"
    export VERILATOR_INSTALL_DIR="$prefix"
    export VERILATOR_BUILD_DIR="/tmp/verilator-build-${version}"
    bash "$script"
    rm -rf "$VERILATOR_BUILD_DIR"
  else
    echo "[INFO] Building Verilator via $script into $prefix"
    mkdir -p /home/cva6/tmp
    export VERILATOR_ROOT="$prefix"
    bash "$script"
    rm -rf /home/cva6/tmp/verilator-*
  fi
  fix_verilator_layout "$prefix"
}

write_tools_env() {
  cat > /etc/cva6_tools_path.sh <<'EOF'
export NUM_JOBS="${NUM_JOBS:-4}"
export RISCV=/tools/riscv
export CV_SW_PREFIX="${CV_SW_PREFIX:-riscv-none-elf-}"
export VERILATOR_INSTALL_DIR=/tools/verilator
export VERILATOR_ROOT=/tools/verilator
export VERILATOR_BIN=verilator_bin
export PATH="/tools/verilator/bin:/tools/riscv/bin:$PATH"
for d in /tools/riscv/lib; do
  if [[ -d "$d" ]]; then
    export LIBRARY_PATH="$d${LIBRARY_PATH:+:$LIBRARY_PATH}"
    export LD_LIBRARY_PATH="$d${LD_LIBRARY_PATH:+:$LD_LIBRARY_PATH}"
  fi
done
if [[ -d /tools/verilator/include ]]; then
  export C_INCLUDE_PATH="/tools/verilator/include:/tools/verilator/include/vltstd${C_INCLUDE_PATH:+:$C_INCLUDE_PATH}"
  export CPLUS_INCLUDE_PATH="/tools/verilator/include:/tools/verilator/include/vltstd${CPLUS_INCLUDE_PATH:+:$CPLUS_INCLUDE_PATH}"
fi
EOF
}

verilator_script="$(detect_verilator_script)"
required_verilator="$(detect_verilator_version "$verilator_script")"
if [[ -z "$verilator_script" || -z "$required_verilator" ]]; then
  echo "[ERROR] Unable to determine required Verilator version"
  exit 1
fi

if selected_verilator_dir="$(preinstalled_verilator_dir "$required_verilator" 2>/dev/null)"; then
  if [[ ! -x "$selected_verilator_dir/bin/verilator" ]]; then
    build_verilator_on_demand "$verilator_script" "$required_verilator" "$selected_verilator_dir"
  else
    echo "[INFO] Reusing preinstalled Verilator $required_verilator from $selected_verilator_dir"
    fix_verilator_layout "$selected_verilator_dir"
  fi
else
  selected_verilator_dir="/tools/verilator-$required_verilator"
  if [[ ! -x "$selected_verilator_dir/bin/verilator" ]]; then
    build_verilator_on_demand "$verilator_script" "$required_verilator" "$selected_verilator_dir"
  else
    echo "[INFO] Reusing dynamically installed Verilator from $selected_verilator_dir"
    fix_verilator_layout "$selected_verilator_dir"
  fi
fi

ln -sfn "$selected_verilator_dir" /tools/verilator
write_tools_env

if ! grep -q "/etc/cva6_tools_path.sh" /etc/cva6_bash_env; then
  echo "source /etc/cva6_tools_path.sh" >> /etc/cva6_bash_env
fi

source /etc/cva6_bash_env
source /etc/cva6_tools_path.sh

echo "[INFO] Verilator ready: $(verilator --version | head -n1)"
echo "[INFO] Toolchain ready: $(riscv-none-elf-gcc --version | head -n1)"
problem_statement:
## Description
In `issue_read_operands`, CVA6 does not always preserve the full 32-bit original instruction for instructions sent through the CVXIF offload path, the interface used to hand an issued instruction to the extension/offload unit. In the failing case, the value forwarded for that instruction can collapse to a 1-bit value instead of the instruction word that was actually issued.

## Expected Behavior
When a CVXIF offload instruction is issued, the original 32-bit instruction associated with that same issue port must be forwarded unchanged. If that stored instruction is later reported through the offload interface or reused for trap reporting, it must exactly match the instruction that triggered the operation.

## Actual Behavior
The design can forward `0` or `1` instead of the real instruction encoding. A reported symptom is that trapping on a floating-point instruction while the FPU is disabled can produce `mtval = 1` instead of the original instruction value, for example `0x0002b007`.

## Affected Function
The bug affects original-instruction handling for the CVXIF offload path in `issue_read_operands`.

## Trigger Condition
The issue is triggered when an instruction is issued through the CVXIF offload path and CVA6 needs to preserve the original instruction word for that issued operation, including the reproduced case where the instruction is accepted on issue port 0.

problem_statement:
## Description
CVA6 uses a shared translation lookaside buffer (shared TLB) to cache page translations and refill the instruction and data TLBs. The shared TLB lookup can report a hit even when no single cached entry matches the entire request. If one way in a set matches the requested virtual page and a different way matches the requested address-space identifier (ASID), the lookup can incorrectly treat that as a valid hit and return a translation from the wrong address space.

## Expected Behavior
A shared TLB hit is valid only when one cached entry matches all lookup fields for the current request. At minimum, the requested virtual page and the ASID must match in the same entry; if additional virtualization qualifiers are enabled for that translation context, those qualifiers must also match in that same entry. If no single entry satisfies the full lookup, the shared TLB must miss so that CVA6 refills the instruction or data TLB from the correct translation.

## Actual Behavior
The lookup can combine partial matches from different ways in the same set and report a false hit. As a result, CVA6 can return a cached translation even though the ASID of the request does not match the entry that supplied the translation.

## Affected Functionality
Shared TLB hit-detection and tag-match logic in the CVA6 memory-management unit (MMU), specifically the logic that decides whether a cached translation can be used to refill the instruction-side or data-side TLB.

## Trigger Condition
The bug appears when a shared-TLB set contains multiple valid entries with different ASIDs. A concrete failing case is: one way holds virtual page X for ASID 0, another way in the same set holds a different virtual page for ASID 1, and a lookup is performed for virtual page X under ASID 1. That lookup must miss because no single entry matches both X and ASID 1, but the buggy logic can report a hit.

problem_statement:
## Description
In CVA6, the memory management unit (MMU) translates virtual addresses for load and store requests from the load/store unit (LSU). When an LSU request already carries a valid misaligned-address exception, that request should be treated as faulting immediately. Instead, the load/store translation path can still start data-side address translation and produce a page-table memory access for the same request.

## Expected Behavior
If the LSU presents a load or store together with a valid misaligned-address exception, the MMU must return the misaligned exception for that access and stop the translation flow for that request. The same access must not trigger a data-side translation lookup or any page-table memory request.

## Actual Behavior
With load/store address translation enabled, a misaligned LSU request can still initiate translation-side activity and generate an observable page-table memory access even though the request is already being reported as misaligned.

## Affected Function
The affected functionality is the MMU load/store address-translation path, specifically the gating between LSU requests that already carry an exception and the data-side translation/page-table access path.

## Trigger Condition
The bug is triggered when load/store virtual-address translation is enabled and the LSU submits a load or store request that already has a valid misaligned-address exception.

#!/bin/bash
set -u

cd /home/cva6 || exit 1

TEST_NAME="cv64a60ax_config_contract"
TB_DIR="/home/cva6/.tb_cv64a60ax_config"
BUILD_LOG="$TB_DIR/build.log"
RUN_LOG="$TB_DIR/run.log"

rm -rf "$TB_DIR"
mkdir -p "$TB_DIR"

VERILATOR_SCRIPT=""
if [ -f "verif/regress/install-verilator.sh" ]; then
  VERILATOR_SCRIPT="verif/regress/install-verilator.sh"
elif [ -f "ci/install-verilator.sh" ]; then
  VERILATOR_SCRIPT="ci/install-verilator.sh"
fi

VERILATOR_HASH=""
if [ -n "$VERILATOR_SCRIPT" ]; then
  VERILATOR_HASH="$(sed -n 's/.*VERILATOR_HASH="\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p' "$VERILATOR_SCRIPT" | head -n 1)"
fi

VERILATOR_PREFIX=""
if [ -n "$VERILATOR_HASH" ] && [ -d "/tools/verilator-$VERILATOR_HASH" ]; then
  VERILATOR_PREFIX="/tools/verilator-$VERILATOR_HASH"
elif [ -d "/tools/verilator" ]; then
  VERILATOR_PREFIX="/tools/verilator"
fi

if [ -n "$VERILATOR_PREFIX" ] && [ -d "$VERILATOR_PREFIX/bin" ]; then
  export PATH="$VERILATOR_PREFIX/bin:$PATH"
  if [ -d "$VERILATOR_PREFIX/share/verilator" ]; then
    export VERILATOR_ROOT="$VERILATOR_PREFIX/share/verilator"
  else
    export VERILATOR_ROOT="$VERILATOR_PREFIX"
  fi
fi

# The xPack wrapper in this image mis-resolves absolute VERILATOR_BIN values.
# Use the real binary directly when available and point VERILATOR_ROOT at the
# data directory so generated makefiles can resolve helper scripts correctly.
unset VERILATOR_BIN

VERILATOR_CMD=""
for candidate in \
  "$VERILATOR_PREFIX/bin/verilator_bin" \
  "$VERILATOR_PREFIX/bin/verilator" \
  "/tools/verilator/bin/verilator_bin" \
  "/tools/verilator/bin/verilator" \
  "$(command -v verilator_bin 2>/dev/null)" \
  "$(command -v verilator 2>/dev/null)"; do
  if [ -n "$candidate" ] && [ -x "$candidate" ]; then
    VERILATOR_CMD="$candidate"
    break
  fi
done

if [ -z "$VERILATOR_CMD" ]; then
  echo "ERROR: unable to locate a runnable Verilator binary" >"$BUILD_LOG"
  echo "HWE_BENCH_RESULTS_START"
  echo "TEST: $TEST_NAME ... FAIL"
  echo "HWE_BENCH_RESULTS_END"
  exit 1
fi

cat > "$TB_DIR/tb.sv" <<'EOF'
`include "core/include/config_pkg.sv"
`include "core/include/cv64a60ax_config_pkg.sv"
`include "core/include/build_config_pkg.sv"
`include "verif/core-v-verif/lib/uvm_agents/uvma_axi5/src/uvma_axi_macros.sv"

module tb_top;
  localparam config_pkg::cva6_cfg_t CVA6Cfg = build_config_pkg::build_config(cva6_config_pkg::cva6_cfg);

  task automatic expect_equal_int(string what, int expected, int got);
    if (expected != got) begin
      $display("CHECK_FAIL %s expected=%0d got=%0d", what, expected, got);
      $fatal(1, "Mismatch for %s", what);
    end
  endtask

  task automatic expect_exec_region(string what, logic [63:0] addr);
    if (!config_pkg::is_inside_execute_regions(CVA6Cfg, addr)) begin
      $display("CHECK_FAIL %s addr=0x%016h", what, addr);
      $fatal(1, "Address outside execute regions: %s", what);
    end
  endtask

  initial begin
    expect_equal_int("axi_addr_width", CVA6Cfg.AxiAddrWidth, `UVMA_AXI_ADDR_MAX_WIDTH);
    expect_equal_int("axi_data_width", CVA6Cfg.AxiDataWidth, `UVMA_AXI_DATA_MAX_WIDTH);
    expect_equal_int("axi_user_width", CVA6Cfg.AxiUserWidth, `UVMA_AXI_USER_MAX_WIDTH);
    expect_equal_int("axi_id_width", CVA6Cfg.AxiIdWidth, `UVMA_AXI_ID_MAX_WIDTH);

    expect_exec_region("dram_hi", 64'h1_0000_0000);

problem_statement:
## Description
`cv64a60ax` is a predefined CVA6 core configuration. In this configuration, two parts of the compile-time contract are inconsistent. First, the AXI bus width macros that downstream verification or integration code reads can disagree with the AXI address, data, user, and ID widths in the generated CVA6 configuration object. Second, `cv64a60ax` declares multiple executable address regions, but executable-address classification only treats the first configured region as executable.

## Expected Behavior
For `cv64a60ax`, the AXI width macros and the generated CVA6 configuration must expose the same AXI address, data, user, and ID widths. Also, if an address falls inside any executable region configured for `cv64a60ax`, the executable-region check must report that address as executable.

## Actual Behavior
When `cv64a60ax` is used, downstream code can observe AXI macro widths that do not match the generated configuration. In addition, addresses that lie in executable regions after the first configured region are reported as non-executable.

## Affected Function
This affects the `cv64a60ax` configuration definition and the logic that exports its AXI interface parameters and executable-region information to the rest of the design and verification environment.

## Trigger Condition
The bug appears when building or verifying CVA6 with the `cv64a60ax` configuration in an environment that consumes the AXI width macros, or when executable-region checks are performed for any configured executable region beyond the first one.

resolved_issues.body: ### Is there an existing CVA6 bug for this? - [x] I have searched the existing bug issues ### Bug Description Some 16 bits illegal instructions (because of a specific bit) can be decoded as C.sh, which is part of the Zcb extension. ## RISC-V Specification Unprivileged ISA: [20250508](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1uviu1nH-tScFfgrovvFCrj7Omv8tFtkp/view) | Privileged Architecture: [20250508](https://drive.google.com/file/d/17GeetSnT5wW3xNuAHI95-SI1gPGd5sJ_/view) | SAIL Model: [20250709](https://github.com/riscv/sail-riscv/tree/63661df518d18ae71b117245775373b9b21e5a3b) ## Example scenario In the CV32A60X configuration, the first instruction that is decoded is `0x8C7C` at t_id (`t##2`). Which can be read as : ` F3 sh r1 r2 c0` `100 011 000 1 1 111 00` Here, the 7th bit is 1 instead of 0 but the instruction is decoded as a C.sh, translated as `sh x15, 2(x8)` and then successfully executed throughout the pipeline until it is commited at t_wb11 (`t##5`). --------------- branch: [cv32a60x](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/tree/cv32a60x) | targeted configuration: cv32a60x | targeted design: cva6_pipeline.sv ------------------- Product: Questa OneSpin Solutions App: Questa Processor App Tool's version: 2025.1

problem_statement:
## Description
CVA6 incorrectly accepts an illegal 16-bit encoding as `C.sh`, the RISC-V Zcb compressed store-halfword instruction. In the failing case, the instruction matches the `C.sh` format except that instruction bit 6 is `1`. Instead of rejecting the encoding, the compressed-instruction decoder expands it into a normal `sh` instruction, so the store executes and retires as if the input were a legal `C.sh`.

## Expected Behavior
For `C.sh`, instruction bit 6 is required to be `0`. If a 16-bit instruction otherwise matches the `C.sh` encoding, then bit 6 = `0` must decode as a legal `C.sh`, while bit 6 = `1` must be marked as an illegal compressed instruction and must not expand into a valid store-halfword operation.

## Actual Behavior
An encoding such as `0x8c7c` is decoded as a legal `C.sh` and translated into `sh x15, 2(x8)`, so software observes a real halfword store where the ISA requires an illegal-instruction exception.

## Affected Function
The bug affects the compressed-instruction decode path that recognizes the Zcb `C.sh` instruction.

## Trigger Condition
The issue occurs when the implementation supports the Zcb `C.sh` instruction and the decoder receives a 16-bit instruction in the `C.sh` encoding family with instruction bit 6 set to `1`.

problem_statement:
## Description
The CVA6 Instruction Trace Interface (ITI) logic in `core/cva6_iti/iti.sv` contains an inferred latch in the combinational generation of `valid_o`. When one cycle produces a valid ITI output and a later cycle on the same output bit should not produce any ITI output, `valid_o` can retain its previous asserted value instead of reflecting only the current inputs.

## Expected Behavior
`valid_o` must be fully determined by the current-cycle inputs on every combinational path. If the current cycle does not produce an ITI record for a given output bit, that `valid_o` bit must be `0`, and the logic must not depend on stored state or an inferred latch to preserve a previous value.

## Actual Behavior
Because `valid_o` is not assigned on all combinational paths, static analysis reports an inferred latch. As a result, `valid_o` can remain high after a previous ITI-producing cycle even when the current cycle should not mark any ITI output as valid.

## Affected Function
The bug affects the output-valid generation logic for the CVA6 Instruction Trace Interface in `core/cva6_iti/iti.sv`.

## Trigger Condition
The issue is triggered by a transition from a cycle that generates a valid ITI output to a following cycle in which no ITI output should be generated for the same output bit.

resolved_issues.title: Possible exception overwrite in pmp_data_if.sv
resolved_issues.body:
I noticed that pmp_data_if.sv does not check whether there is an existing exception occurring earlier in the pipeline. It seems to thus be possible that the PMP can overwrite an existing exception. The specific case that I am observing is that I get a kernel crash at the first instruction of user mode during Linux boot.

The process I believe is occurring is:
1. First instruction begins fetch
2. Walk of PTW hits a PTE that exists but Linux hasn't mapped the PTE yet, so it throws a page fault. The PA field in the core is not valid at this point, but the garbage PA is still sent to the PMP
3. The PMP evaluates the garbage PA and finds that it's outside the executable region (either PMP configured or PMA configured) and overwrites the existing exception with an INSTR_ACCESS_FAULT
4. The OS sees this fault instead of a page fault and thus kills the process instead of simply mapping the unmapped page

When I overwrite the line below to also check `!icache_areq_i.fetch_exception.valid`, the kernel crash does not occur. Note that I also add a check of `icache_areq_i.fetch_valid` because otherwise the PMP could potentially raise an exception based on another spurious PA that it gets fed which seems like a questionable interface.

https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blame/9a266a5521e3c25dd1d887b0a5b68a446a84315f/core/pmp/src/pmp_data_if.sv#L81

I see git blame on the line above from @OlivierBetschi though that may just be due to the PMP refactor.

problem_statement:
## Description
The instruction-fetch protection logic in `pmp_data_if.sv` can still evaluate PMP/PMA execute permissions for a fetch that is not valid, or for a fetch that has already raised an instruction page fault during address translation. In the reported Linux boot scenario, this causes the first user-mode instruction fetch to be reported as `INSTR_ACCESS_FAULT` instead of the original `INSTR_PAGE_FAULT`.

## Expected Behavior
The instruction-fetch PMP/PMA check should only report `INSTR_ACCESS_FAULT` for a valid fetch request. An invalid fetch request must not generate a new instruction exception. If address translation has already raised `INSTR_PAGE_FAULT` for the fetch, that page fault must remain the reported exception and must not be replaced by `INSTR_ACCESS_FAULT`.

## Actual Behavior
`pmp_data_if.sv` can run the execute-permission check even when the fetch request is invalid or when the fetch already carries an `INSTR_PAGE_FAULT`. If the physical address presented to PMP/PMA at that point is stale, incomplete, or otherwise not the final translated fetch address, the check can raise `INSTR_ACCESS_FAULT` and overwrite the page-fault result.

## Affected Function
Instruction-fetch PMP/PMA execute-permission checking in `pmp_data_if.sv`.

## Trigger Condition
The bug is triggered on the instruction-fetch path when the fetch is not yet valid, or when page-table translation has already produced `INSTR_PAGE_FAULT` before a reliable physical fetch address is available. In that state, the PMP/PMA logic can evaluate a bogus fetch physical address and report the wrong trap cause.

title: Fix a bug that causes the core to freeze when enabling CV-X-IF while disabling RVC extension
body:
This is an attempt to fix the bug described in #3167.

It appears that when enabling the CV-X-IF interface while disabling the RVC extension, the core freezes during the initialization phase of the debug sequence in the testbench.

I managed to find out that this was caused by a bug inside the Decode stage: the compressed‑instruction channel driver of the CV-X-IF inside the Decode stage is only generated if the RVC extension is enabled. However, this module still drives signals inside the stage even when RVC is off. I proposed a fix in the PR below, although I am not sure it is the cleanest way to address the issue.

problem_statement:
## Description
CVA6 can lose forward progress when the CV-X-IF interface for custom extensions is enabled while the RVC extension, the RISC-V compressed-instruction extension, is disabled. In this configuration, the Decode stage can still let the CV-X-IF compressed-instruction path affect instruction decoding even though compressed instructions are not supported. The failure was observed during debug-sequence initialization, where the core freezes instead of continuing execution.

## Expected Behavior
When RVC is disabled, a fetched instruction must be handled as a normal 32-bit uncompressed instruction. Enabling CV-X-IF in that configuration must not block decode, prevent a valid decode result from being issued, change the forwarded 32-bit instruction value, or mark the instruction as compressed.

## Actual Behavior
With CV-X-IF enabled and RVC disabled, the Decode stage may incorrectly let the compressed-instruction path participate in decode. As a result, an ordinary 32-bit instruction can fail to produce a valid issued decode result or be treated as compressed, which causes the core to stop making forward progress.

## Affected Function
Decode-stage handling of the interaction between the normal instruction-decode path and the CV-X-IF compressed-instruction path.

## Trigger Condition
The bug is triggered when CV-X-IF is enabled in a CVA6 configuration that disables RVC, and the core decodes a regular 32-bit instruction, including early instructions seen during debug-sequence initialization.

resolved_issues.title: [BUG] some bitmanip instructions decoder lacks bit-field validation
resolved_issues.body: ### Is there an existing CVA6 bug for this? - [x] I have searched the existing bug issues ### Bug Description **Bug Description** Hello, this is an RTL bug in the CVA6 Decoder. The problem appears in the CPOPW、CTZW、CLZW instructions decoding logic. There is problem here: 1. There's no condition for bits [24:22]. According to the spec (CPOPW), these should always be 0 (the complete field bits [24:20] must be 5'b00010, not just bits [21:20] == 2'b10). https://riscv.github.io/riscv-isa-manual/snapshot/unprivileged/#insns-cpopw So if we try using a directed test to execute a (CPOPW、CTZW、CLZW) instructions with bits [24:22] != 3'b000, the RTL will still execute it https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/issues/2276. This #2276 bug issue led to the discovery and fixing of several other B-extension instructions,However, the bug in these (CPOPW、CTZW、CLZW) instructions have not yet been patched.

problem_statement:
## Description
CVA6 incorrectly accepts illegal encodings of the RISC-V Zbb word bit-manipulation instructions `CLZW`, `CTZW`, and `CPOPW`. For these instructions, bits `[24:22]` are reserved and must be `000`, so legality depends on the full `[24:20]` field rather than only on bits `[21:20]`. In the current decoder behavior, encodings with nonzero bits `[24:22]` can alias to these legal instructions instead of being rejected.

## Expected Behavior
When decoding `CLZW`, `CTZW`, and `CPOPW`, CVA6 must treat the instruction as legal only when the full `[24:20]` field matches the architecturally defined encoding for that operation. If bits `[24:22]` are not `000`, the decoder must raise an illegal-instruction exception.

## Actual Behavior
If an instruction otherwise matches the `CLZW`/`CTZW`/`CPOPW` decode pattern and bits `[21:20]` select one of those operations, CVA6 still decodes it as legal even when bits `[24:22]` are nonzero. Illegal encodings are therefore accepted by the decoder instead of being flagged as illegal instructions.

## Affected Function
The affected logic is the CVA6 decoder handling of the RISC-V Zbb word bit-manipulation instructions `CLZW`, `CTZW`, and `CPOPW`.

## Trigger Condition
This bug is triggered by `CLZW`, `CTZW`, or `CPOPW`-like encodings whose bits `[21:20]` select one of those operations while bits `[24:22]` are not `000`.

title: Fix the Meltdown and Spectre vulnerabilities that break the isolation between user-space and kernel-space
body:
This PR is to fix the https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/issues/3163 and https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/issues/3190. 

This fix has prohibited the result of the instruction with exception from being forwarding to subsequent instructions in the scoreboard. This ensures that the kernel-space data cannot be transmitted to the user-space code, thereby preventing the secret from being encoded into the microarchitecture.

By invalidating the corresponding [`fwd_res_valid`](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/issue_read_operands.sv#L541) entry for the scoreboard entries with exceptions, it is possible to defend against attacks of Meltdown, Spectre and their variants.

resolved_issues.title: [BUG] An exploitable Meltdown vulnerability was found in CVA6
resolved_issues.body: ### Is there an existing CVA6 bug for this? - [x] I have searched the existing bug issues ### Bug Description Hi! Our processor side-channel vulnerability detection work has found an efficient and fault-tolerant Meltdown vulnerability on CVA6, which allows an attacker to leak kernel-space data at arbitrary addresses from user space. This vulnerability takes advantage of the feature of the CVA6 scoreboard: in-flight intructions in the scoreboard won’t trigger exceptions until they commit. Thus, we can access privilege data in a transient execution window and encode the privileged data in the microarchitecture. We provide an end-to-end exploit code and vulnerability explanation below. ```asm 2f40: fdiv.d fa5,fa5,fa4 2f44: lb t1, 0(a0) # a0 contains secret address 0xffffffffffe06f30, secret data is 0x30 2f48: slli t1, t1, 5 # encode secret to a probe array (index = secret << 5, t1 = 0x30 << 5 = 0x600) 2f4c: add t0, t1, t0 # encode secret to a probe array (base = 0x10000, t0 = base + t1 = 0x10600) 2f50: ld t1, 0(t0) # encode the secret to cache ``` The code runs under U-mode. The `lb` at `0x2f44` tries to access `0xffffffffffe06f30`, which is a kernel-space address. After the secret data is loaded, it will be encoded into the cache through the user-space array with the base address of `0x10000`. Due to the long latency of `fdiv` and the function [unit ready status](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/issue_read_operands.sv#L413), subsequent instructions will be issued during the `fdiv` transition execution window, as the waveform shows. **G1** represents the commit signals, **G2** represents scoreboard entries and **G3** represents the LSU, Dcache and memory bus behaviors. The first `lsu_valid_i` is triggered by `lb`, and the access address is successfully translated. The secret data is read from the Dcache and forwarded to the scoreboard. Thus, the `slli` and `add` can be issued in sequence. Finally, the secret is encoded in `t0`, which is the load address of` ld` at `0x2f50`. This is a cache-miss address. Thus, Dcache will fill the cacheline by initiating a memory access, as observed in `io_axi4_0_ar_valid`. All of the above processes take place within the `fdiv` transient execution window. In fact, when executing the `lb` at `0x2f44` architecturally, a load page fault exception will be triggered, and `t1` result will be 0. However, this is not important. We have already encoded the secret in the microarchitecture. Then we try to probe whether we successfully encoded the secret into the cache. The code sequentially accessed the memory addresses `0x105e0`, `0x10600`, `0x10620`, and `0x10640`. These addresses belong to different cachelines. ```asm probe: li t0, 0x10600 2f7c: ld t1, -32(t0) # cache miss 2f80: ld t1, 0(t0) # cache hit, addr = 0x10000 + 0x30 << 5 2f84: ld t1, 32(t0) # cache miss 2f88: ld t1, 64(t0) # cache miss ``` As shown in the waveform, compared with the `ld` that accesses `0x10600`, all the other `ld` have significantly longer execution times and all exhibit bus memory access behavior. Therefore, through the time side-channel, we can recover the aforementioned secret data. It is worth noting that this vulnerability has a high level of **fault tolerance**. Even if the secret address results in a TLB miss, this transient window is long enough to complete the Page Table Walk process. Similarly, if the address of the probe array also results in a TLB miss, the Page Table Walk can still be completed, and the secret can be encoded in the TLB. This vulnerability can be reproduced at the master commit aa4f5a548b33f7edff63483347fc8510aa9ad5fd and the default cv64a6_imafdc_sv39 config. The full elf file are provided below. [rv64_test-av-CVA6-meltdown-fdiv.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/24147141/rv64_test-av-CVA6-meltdown-fdiv.zip)

resolved_issues.title: [BUG] Spectre-type Vulnerability and Its Different Variants were Found in CVA6
resolved_issues.body: ### Is there an existing CVA6 bug for this? - [x] I have searched the existing bug issues ## Summary We creatively used `ecall` to delay the resolution of the branch, creating a branch misprediction transient window. In this window, we can access kernel-space data and encode it in different microarchitecture components at U-mode without exception. ## Bug Description Hi! Our processor side-channel vulnerability detection work has found Spectre vulnerability and its different variants on CVA6, which allows an attacker to leak kernel-space data from user space without exception. CVA6 employs thie Scoreboard for out-of-order issuing. The Scoreboard algorithm won't issue instructions that have RAW conflicts. Therefore, when a B-type instruction is issued, its operands are already ready. So, B-type instructions can be resolved very quickly. As a result, the traditional Spectre vulnerabilities cannot perform the secret access and encoding operation within the CVA6's 1-2 cycles branch midprediction window. However, we creatively introduce `ecall` to delay the resolution of the branch. `ecall` is a instruction that will implicitly write register `a0`. But in the implementation of CVA6 Scoreboard, `ecall` won't be in conflict with the subsequent instructions that take `a0` as an operand. This give us a chance to issue B-type instruction with operand `a0`. CVA6 will read the old value of `a0` and make a wrong descision on the B-type instrucion. Then, we accessed and encoded the secret on the wrong branch. This takes advantage of the feature of the CVA6 Scoreboard: in-flight intructions in the scoreboard won’t trigger exceptions until they commit, which we have illustrated in detail in previous issue: [An exploitable Meltdown vulnerability was found in CVA6](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/issues/3163). We provide an end-to-end exploit code and vulnerability explanation below. ``` 2f40: fdiv.d fa5, fa5, fa4 2f44: ecall # overwrite a0 to a non-zero value 2f48: bnez a0, 2f84 # the old value of a0 is zero 2f4c: lb t0, 0(a1) # a1 contains secret address 0xffffffffffe04000 2f50: slli t0, t0, 0x5 # use secret as index 2f54: add t0, t1, t0 # t1 contains probe array address 0x10000 2f58: ld t1, 0(t0) # encode secret to probe array ... 2f84 : # the true control flow will jump to here ... ``` The code runs under U-mode. `a0` is initialized to 0. The `lb` at `0x2f4c` tries to access `0xffffffffffe04000`, which is a kernel-space address. After the secret data is loaded, it will be encoded into the cache through the user-space array with the base address of `0x10000`. Due to the long latency of fdiv and the misprediction of `bnez`, subsequent instructions will be issued during the transition execution window, as the waveform shows. **G1** represents the [commit signals](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/scoreboard.sv#L100).**G2** represents [Scoreboard entries](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/scoreboard.sv#L100). **G3** represents the LSU, Dcache and memory bus behaviors, including [`lsu_valid_i`](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/load_store_unit.sv#L52), [`vaddr_o`](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/load_store_unit.sv#L575), [`paddr_i`](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/load_store_unit.sv#L579), [`miss_o`](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/cache_subsystem/wt_dcache.sv#L37), [`mem_rtrn_vld_i`](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/cache_subsystem/wt_dcache.sv#L51), `io_axi4_0_ar_valid`, `io_axi4_0_ar_bits_addr` and `io_axi4_0_r_valid`. The first `lsu_valid_i` is triggered by `lb`, and the access address is successfully translated. The secret data is read from the Dcache and forwarded to the Scoreboard. Thus, the `slli` and `add` can be issued in sequence. Finally, the secret is encoded in `t0`, which is the load address of `ld` at `0x2f58`. This is a cache-miss address. Thus, Dcache will fill the cacheline by initiating a memory access, as observed in `io_axi4_0_ar_valid`. All of the above processes take place within the `fdiv` transient execution window. After `ecall` trap process finished, `a0` will be modified to a non-zero value. `bnez` at `0x2f48` will taken and control flow will skip these instructions between `0x2f4c` and `0x2f58`. But these instructions have been microarchitecturally executed. Then we try to probe whether we successfully encoded the secret into the cache. The code sequentially accessed the memory addresses `0x10000`, `0x10010`, `0x10020`, and `0x10030`. These addresses belong to different cachelines. ``` 5000: lui t0, 0x10 5004: ld t1, 0(t0) # t0 = 0x10000 5008: ld t1, 16(t0) 500c: ld t1, 32(t0) 5010: ld t1, 48(t0) ``` As shown in the waveform, compared with the `ld` that accesses `0x10020`, all the other `ld` have significantly longer execution times and all exhibit bus memory access behavior. Therefore, through the time side-channel, we can recover the aforementioned secret data. This vulnerability can be reproduced at the master commit [aa4f5a5](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/commit/aa4f5a548b33f7edff63483347fc8510aa9ad5fd) and the default cv64a6_imafdc_sv39 config. The full elf file are provided below. ## Variants In CVA6, not only the DCache can be used as a component for encoding and decoding secrets. We have discovered that the frontend states, such as BTB, BHT, RAS, etc., can be changed within the transient window. And after the speculation execution was rolled back, these states will not be rolled back. Thus, secrets can be encoded in these front-end components. ### BTB [BTB](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/frontend/btb.sv#L28) is a frontend branch prediction unit. It provides branch prediction for `jalr` instructions except for `call` and `ret`. BTB will record the target addresses of these `jalr` instructions, and when it encounters the corresponding `jalr` again in the future, it will directly predict the jump address to be the recorded target address. As shown in the following code, we have constructed a jump address that depends on the secret. Depending on the secret, the target address for the `jalr` instruction located at `0x2f58` will change. During the transient window, after the `jalr` target jump address is calculated, the BTB entries will be updated. After the transient window rollback, the BTB entries will not be invalidated, so we will keep the secret in the BTB. ``` 2f40: fdiv.d fa5, fa5, fa4 2f44: ecall 2f48: bnez a0, 80002f9c 2f4c: lb t0, 0(a1) # a1 contains secret address 2f50: slli t0, t0, 0x2 2f54: add t1, t1, t0 # t1 contains probe address 2f58 : 2f58: jalr t0, t1 # train the btb, different secret will reseult in different target address ... 2f8c : 2f8c: nop 2f90: nop 2f94: nop 2f98: nop ... ``` As shown in the following two waveform figures. We changed the value of secret and ran the testcase. When the secret is 0, the predicted jump address of the corresponding entry in the BTB will be updated to `2f8c`. When the secret is 1, the predicted jump address of the corresponding entry in the BTB will be updated to `2f90`. **G5** represents [BTB update signals](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/frontend/btb.sv#L45). **secret = 0** **secret != 0** Next, we will attempt to decode the data. Based on the analysis of the [BTB entry matching mechanism](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/frontend/btb.sv#L69), we found that BTB makes predictions only based on the lower bits of the PC, and does not match the entire PC. Therefore, we use the following instruction for decoding. ``` 5000: la t1, probe # t1 = 0x2f8c ... 5058: jalr t0, t1 ``` During the decoding stage, we placed a `jalr` instruction at the address `0x5058`. This address shares the same BTB entry with the `jalr` instruction that previously encoded the secret at `0x2f58`. So it will trigger branch prediction. **G4** represents [BTB prediction signals](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/frontend/btb.sv#L47). If the secret is 0, then the branch prediction is correct and the execution time is shorter. If the secret is 1, then the branch prediction is incorrect and the execution time will be slower. So this creates a timing side-channel. **secret = 0** **secret != 0** ### BHT [BHT](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/frontend/bht.sv) is also a frontend branch predictor. It records the jump situations of the B-type instructions. When it encounters the corresponding B-type instructions again, it makes branch prediction based on the recorded historical information. This BHT uses a 2-bit [saturation counter](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/frontend/bht.sv#L56) to record the historical taken/untaken situations. If a B-type instruction is taken, the saturation counter of the corresponding entry is incremented by one. When the value of the saturation counter is greater than or equal to 2, it predicts that the B-type instruction will be taken in the future. We conduct the following testcase. The `beqz` instruction at `0x2f50` is taken/untaken based on whether the secret is zero. We use this instruction to encode the secret. ``` 2f40: fdiv.d fa5, fa5, fa4 2f44: ecall 2f48: bnez a0, 2f80 2f4c: lb t0, 0(a1) # a1 contains secret address 2f50: 2f50: beqz t0, 2f7c # train BHT ... 2f7c : ``` The two waveform diagrams below illustrate the encoding stages under different secrets. **G5** represents the [BHT entry](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/frontend/bht.sv#L59) corresponding to the `beqz` instruction. When the secret is 0, the `beqz` instruction is taken and updates the corresponding saturation counter to 1. When the secret is 1, the `beqz` instruction is untaken, and the saturation counter for the corresponding entry remains unchanged and stays at 0. **secret = 0** **secret != 0** We use the following instructions to decode the secret. Similar to BTB, BHT also only matches the lower bits of the PC to determine a BHT entry. We placed a `beqz` instruction at the address `0x5050`. This instruction will use the same BHT entry as the `beqz` instruction that encodes secret at address `0x2f50`. We set `t0` to 0 so that the `beqz` instruction will be taken. Then we observe the behavior of the `beqz` instruction at address 0x5050 at its second time execution. ``` 5000: li t0, 0 ... 5050: beqz t0, 5000 ``` **G4** represents the [BHT prediction result](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/frontend/bht.sv#L42) for the `beqz` instruction at address `0x5050`. When the secret is 0, this BHT entry records two branch takens. Therefore, when the instruction at `0x5050` is executed for the second time, the BHT will predicte it to be taken. The branch prediction is correct and the execution time is faster. When the secret is 1, this BHT entry records only one branch taken. The BHT will predicte it to be untaken. The branch prediction is incorrect and the execution time slows down. This forms a timing side-channel. **secret = 0** **secret != 0** ### RAS [RAS](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/frontend/ras.sv) is used to push the return address onto the stack when making a call. We attempted to utilize RAS to create a temporal side-channel. By performing secret-dependent RAS operations within the transient window, the secret is encoded within the RAS. After the transient window rollback, the status of RAS will not be revoked. This enables the decoding of the secret. In the following testcase, `ra` is influenced by the secret. If the secret is 0, then the `jalr` instruction located at `0x2f58` will be executed. Executing this instruction will push the address of the next instruction into RAS, thereby changing the state of RAS. If the secret is not zero, then `0x2f58` will be skipped and the state of RAS will not be changed. ``` 2f40: fdiv.d fa5, fa5,fa4 2f44: ecall 2f48: bnez a0, 2fb0 2f4c: lb t0, 0(a1) # a1 contains secret address 2f50: add ra, t2, t0 # t2 is initialized to 0x2f58. RAS top = previous call address + 4 2f54: ret # pop RAS. if t0 == 0, continue to execute 0x2f58 2f58: jalr ra, t3 # push 0x2f5c into RAS. RAS top = 0x2f5c ``` **G4** represents the RAS-related signal. Including the push signal [`push_i`](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/frontend/ras.sv#L29), the data pushed onto the stack [`data_i`](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/frontend/ras.sv#L33), the pop signal [`pop_i`](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/frontend/ras.sv#L31), the valid signal indicating the availability of the top stack data [`data_o.valid`](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/frontend/ras.sv#L35), and the data at the top of the stack [`data_o.ra`](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/frontend/ras.sv#L35). When the secret is 0, the `jalr` instruction at `0x2f58` within the transient window is executed, pushing `0x2f5c` into the stack. When the secret is not 0, the state of RAS has not changed. **secret = 0** **secret != 0** We use the following code to decode the secret. We execute an instruction that returns to `0x2f5c`. At this point, RAS is used for target address prediction. This address is precisely the value that was pushed into RAS when the secret was 0. ``` 5000: li ra, 0x2f5c 5008: ret ``` Observe the ret instruction located at 0x5008. If the value of "secret" is 0, the prediction is correct and the execution time is fast. If the value of "secret" is not 0, the prediction will be incorrect and the execution time will be slow. This forms a timing side-channel. **secret = 0** **secret != 0** ### ICache All the instructions executed by CVA6 come from the [ICache](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/cache_subsystem/cva6_icache.sv). The reading of instructions is strongly related to the control flow. So we attempted to influence the control flow through "secret", thereby affecting the state of the ICache, in order to encode the secret into the ICache. In the following testcase, a secret-dependent `beqz` instruction was placed at the address `0x2f50`. If the secret is 0, it will jump to the `probe` instruction block. It is necessary to ensure beforehand that the `probe` instruction block is not in the ICache. ``` 2f40: fdiv.d fa5, fa5, fa4 2f44: ecall 2f48: bnez a0, 2f90 2f4c: lb t0, 0(a1) 2f50: beqz t0, 2f80 ... 2f80 : ``` **G4** represents the signals related to the ICache, including the ICache miss signal [`miss_o`](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/cache_subsystem/cva6_icache.sv#L50) and the instructions request signal [`areq_i`](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/cache_subsystem/cva6_icache.sv#L52). When the secret is 0, the control flow needs to jump to the `probe` instruction block at address `0x2f80`. Since the `probe` instruction is not located in the ICache, an ICache miss occurred. At this point, the ICache initiates a refill request to the memory. Ultimately, the content of the `probe` instruction block is filled back into the ICache. However, when the secret is not zero, the `probe` instruction block will not be filled into the ICache. **secret = 0** **secret != 0** We directly execute the probe instruction block and observe the execution time. ``` 5000: j 2f80 ``` It can be observed that when the secret is 0, the `probe` instruction block has already been loaded into the ICache during the transient window, so when jumping to the `probe` instruction block, it can be executed directly. However, when the secret is not zero, the `probe` instruction block will not be loaded in the transient window. Thus, an ICache miss occurs and the instruction needs to be fetched from the memory, resulting in a significant time difference. **secret = 0** **secret != 0** ## Conclusion Overall, although CVA6 uses the scoreboard for instruction scheduling and inherently has a relatively small transient execution window, it can still be bypassed in various ways. Moreover, the microarchitecture of CVA6 has numerous timing vulnerabilities. [CVA6-spectre-ecall-dcache.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/24755549/CVA6-spectre-ecall-dcache.zip) [CVA6-spectre-ecall-btb.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/24755552/CVA6-spectre-ecall-btb.zip) [CVA6-spectre-ecall-bht.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/24755554/CVA6-spectre-ecall-bht.zip) [CVA6-spectre-ecall-icache.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/24755556/CVA6-spectre-ecall-icache.zip) [CVA6-spectre-ecall-ras.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/24755557/CVA6-spectre-ecall-ras.zip)

--- a/core/issue_read_operands.sv
+++ b/core/issue_read_operands.sv
@@ -538,7 +538,7 @@ module issue_read_operands
   always_comb begin
     for (int unsigned i = 0; i < CVA6Cfg.NR_SB_ENTRIES; i++) begin
       fwd_res[i] = fwd_i.sbe[i].result;
-      fwd_res_valid[i] = fwd_i.sbe[i].valid;
+      fwd_res_valid[i] = fwd_i.sbe[i].valid & (~fwd_i.sbe[i].ex.valid);

prepare_script:
#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail

export NUM_JOBS="${NUM_JOBS:-4}"

cd /home/cva6
git reset --hard
git clean -fdx
git checkout a5e1e76a549272979bb98b5ae1978a7f378e3017
git submodule sync --recursive
git submodule update --init --recursive

detect_verilator_script() {
  if [[ -f verif/regress/install-verilator.sh ]]; then
    echo "verif/regress/install-verilator.sh"
  elif [[ -f ci/install-verilator.sh ]]; then
    echo "ci/install-verilator.sh"
  fi
}

detect_verilator_version() {
  local script="$1"
  local version=""
  if [[ -n "$script" ]]; then
    version="$(sed -n 's/.*VERILATOR_HASH="\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p' "$script" | head -n1)"
  fi
  echo "$version"
}

build_verilator_on_demand() {
  local script="$1"
  local version="$2"
  local prefix="$3"

  export VERILATOR_INSTALL_DIR="$prefix"
  export VERILATOR_BUILD_DIR="/tmp/verilator-build-${version}"
  bash "$script"
  rm -rf "$VERILATOR_BUILD_DIR"

  if [[ -d "$prefix/share/verilator/include" ]]; then
    ln -sfn "$prefix/share/verilator/include" "$prefix/include"
  fi
}

verilator_script="$(detect_verilator_script)"
required_verilator="$(detect_verilator_version "$verilator_script")"

if [[ -z "$verilator_script" || -z "$required_verilator" ]]; then
  echo "[ERROR] Unable to determine required Verilator version"
  exit 1
fi

problem_statement:
## Description
CVA6 uses a scoreboard to track in-flight instructions and to forward produced register values to younger instructions that have read-after-write (RAW) dependencies. A scoreboard entry that already carries a pending exception can still be treated as a valid forwarding source. Because exceptions from in-flight instructions are not architecturally taken until commit, a younger dependent instruction may issue and consume that result before the trap redirects execution. In user-mode faulting-access scenarios, this allows data from the faulting access to transiently influence later instructions and microarchitectural state.

## Expected Behavior
A scoreboard entry with a pending exception must not satisfy a RAW dependency for a younger instruction. If the older instruction will trap, its destination-register value must not be forwarded or considered ready. The younger dependent instruction should remain blocked until the exception is taken or until a non-exceptional producer supplies the operand.

## Actual Behavior
The scoreboard forwarding path can mark an exceptional in-flight result as available solely because the entry itself is valid. As a result, a younger instruction that reads the producer's destination register can be acknowledged and issued, and it can receive the forwarded value even though the producer will later raise an exception.

## Affected Function
The affected functionality is CVA6's scoreboard-based RAW dependency resolution and operand forwarding between older in-flight instructions and younger dependent instructions.

## Trigger Condition
The bug is triggered when an older in-flight instruction has produced a destination-register result and also has a pending exception, while a younger instruction has a RAW dependency on that destination register. This includes faulting accesses, such as a user-mode load from kernel-space memory, whose transient result is observed before the exception is committed.

problem_statement:
## Description
CVA6's instruction decoder accepts the privileged RISC-V `HFENCE.VVMA` and `HFENCE.GVMA` instructions even when the instruction encoding uses a non-zero `rd` field. For these instructions, the `rd` field is reserved and must be `x0`.

## Expected Behavior
`HFENCE.VVMA` and `HFENCE.GVMA` should decode as legal instructions only when their `rd` field is `x0`. If either instruction is encoded with `rd != x0`, decode must raise an illegal-instruction exception instead of issuing an HFENCE operation. When `rd == x0` and the instruction otherwise satisfies the normal privilege checks, it should decode as the corresponding HFENCE operation.

## Actual Behavior
A non-zero `rd` is ignored once the decoder reaches a privilege context that would otherwise accept the instruction. As a result, malformed `HFENCE.VVMA` and `HFENCE.GVMA` encodings are dispatched as valid operations instead of being rejected as illegal instructions.

## Affected Function
The affected area is the instruction decode logic for the privileged hypervisor fence instructions `HFENCE.VVMA` and `HFENCE.GVMA`, specifically the legality checks for their instruction encodings.

## Trigger Condition
The bug is triggered when software executes `HFENCE.VVMA` or `HFENCE.GVMA` with `rd != x0` in a privilege context where the instruction would otherwise pass the normal privilege checks.

resolved_issues.title: TVAL on misaligned jump/branch should be the target address?
resolved_issues.body:
Currently TVAL is reported as the address of the branch itself on a branch/jump misaligned instruction (redundant with EPC).

https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/301d11ceb88c1169f75e9dea415e4bff4eb29888/core/branch_unit.sv#L123

From the RISC-V privilege spec, it should be the "faulting virtual address", which I would interpret to be the target address that is misaligned, rather than the address of the branch instruction which is already accessible in EPC.

If people agree, I'm happy to file the simple PR to fix it.

resolved_issues.title: [Bug Report] Incorrect *tval for ecall/ebreak
resolved_issues.body:
Our co-simulation framework found that the `*tval` of `ecall/ebreak` is incorrect.
In cva6, after `ecall/ebreak`, *tval will set to the machine code of the `ecall/ebreak` instruction.

In the following test case, after calling `ebreak` in s-mode, the value of `mtval` register is written to `0x100073`, which is the machine code of `ebreak` instruction.

```
[spike] core   0: 0x0000000080000174 (0x00100193) li      gp, 1
[cva6]       664ns      649 S 0000000080000174 0 00100193 li             gp, 1
[cva6]  Exception @     66500, PC: 0000000080000178, Cause: Breakpoint, tval: 0000000000100073
[spike] core   0: 0x0000000080000178 (0x00100073) ebreak
[spike] core   0: exception trap_breakpoint, epc 0x0000000080000178
[spike] core   0:           tval 0x0000000080000178
... /* in handler */
[spike] core   0: 0x0000000080000190 (0x343022f3) csrr    t0, mtval
[error] WDATA SIM 0000000080000178, DUT 0000000000100073
[error] check board clear 5 error
[CJ]  integer register Judge Failed
```

riscv-priviledged P41 ：If `mtval` is written with a nonzero value when a breakpoint, address-misaligned, access-fault, or page-fault exception occurs on an instruction fetch, load, or store, then mtval will contain the faulting virtual address.
According to specifications, `mtval` should be the faulting address (or zero).

Issue [448](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/issues/448) tests the value in `stval` of `ecall` from user mode, our verification framework further discovered that `ebreak` also has the same bug, and both of them could be triggered under **any privilege modes**.

ebreak testcase: [cva6-1.zip](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/files/8832584/cva6-1.zip)
ecall testcase: [cva6-2.zip](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/files/8832585/cva6-2.zip)
> @LuminaDCIX helps reproduce the problem

resolved_issues.title: [BUG] `tval` contain wrong value in case of `breakpoint`
resolved_issues.body:
### Is there an existing CVA6 bug for this?

- [X] I have searched the existing bug issues

### Bug Description

### Bug Description

If `tval` is written with a nonzero value when a **breakpoint**, address-misaligned, access-fault, or page-
fault exception occurs on an instruction fetch, load, or store, then `tval` will contain the faulting virtual address. However, in the latest version of CVA6, the instruction value placed in the `tval`.

Execute following instruction:
```
int main(void){
    asm volatile ("c.ebreak");
    // tval= 0000000000009002 which is the opcode of c.ebreak
}
```

However, if you execute same code on Spike you will get `pc` value in `tval` .

    - Spike version: `1.1.1-dev`
    - version: `CVA6 commit: 7435cb310ee98c246edd15d00ec236ad2c6ff490`
    - OS: `CentOS Linux release 7.9.2009 kernel: 5.15.0-78-generic`
    - Simulator: `VCS_2023`

resolved_issues.title: [BUG] Incorrect TVAL cases in decoder
resolved_issues.body:
### Is there an existing CVA6 bug for this?

- [x] I have searched the existing bug issues

### Bug Description

Further to https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/issues/3018, the following TVAL behaviours currently in CVA6 seem to be illegal from reading the spec.

- ECALL reports the instruction bits in TVAL: it should write zeros
- EBREAK reports the instruction bits in TVAL: it should report the instruction PC (I think that's the "faulting virtual address" in this case?)

These were found by fuzzing against Sail with TestRIG

If people agree, I'm happy to file a PR to fix these.

problem_statement:
## Description
CVA6 writes incorrect values to the trap value CSR (`mtval`/`stval`, collectively `*tval`) for several synchronous exceptions. `*tval` is the exception-specific value that trap handlers read when diagnosing a fault.

## Expected Behavior
For an instruction-address-misaligned exception raised by a taken branch or jump, `*tval` must contain the misaligned target address. For an `ecall` exception, `*tval` must be zero. For an `ebreak` exception, `*tval` must contain the address of the faulting instruction (the program counter of the `ebreak`), not the instruction encoding.

## Actual Behavior
When a taken branch or jump resolves to a misaligned target, CVA6 writes the branch/jump instruction address into `*tval` instead of the misaligned target address. When decoding `ecall` or `ebreak`, CVA6 writes the instruction bits into `*tval`, so trap handlers observe an opcode value where the architecture expects zero for `ecall` or the faulting instruction address for `ebreak`.

## Affected Functionality
The bug affects trap-value (`*tval`) generation for exceptions produced by the control-flow path and by decoding `ecall`/`ebreak`.

## Trigger Condition
The problem appears when a taken branch or jump targets a misaligned instruction address, or when software executes `ecall` or `ebreak` and then inspects `mtval`/`stval` in the resulting trap handler.

title: fix: mstatus.SXL/UXL should be 0 when S/U modes are not implemented
body: This PR fixes #3182 by ensuring the SXL and UXL fields in mstatus are tied to 0 when S-mode or U-mode is not implemented, as required by the RISC-V Privileged Spec.

resolved_issues.title: [BUG] mstatus.SXL/UXL read as XLEN_64 when S-mode/U-mode are not implemented,which violates RISC-V Spec
resolved_issues.body: ### Is there an existing CVA6 bug for this? - [x] I have searched the existing bug issues ### Bug Description ### Description The RISC-V Privileged Specification defines mstatus.SXL and mstatus.UXL as the effective XLEN for S-mode and U-mode. When the corresponding privilege mode is not implemented, these fields should be read-only zero. In CVA6, SXL and UXL are unconditionally assigned to XLEN_64 when IS_XLEN64 is true, regardless of whether S-mode (RVS) or U-mode (RVU) are implemented. ### Spec reference RISC-V Privileged Spec: If S-mode is not supported: SXL is read-only 0 If U-mode is not supported: UXL is read-only 0 ### in CVA6 csr_regfile.sv This makes SXL/UXL appear non-zero in configurations where CVA6Cfg.RVS=0 and/or CVA6Cfg.RVU=0.

problem_statement:
## Description
In RV64 configurations that do not implement supervisor mode and/or user mode, reading `mstatus` reports non-zero values in the `SXL` and `UXL` fields. CVA6 currently exposes these fields as if the missing privilege modes still had an effective XLEN of 64 bits, so software can observe `SXL` and `UXL` as `XLEN_64` even when the corresponding mode does not exist.

## Expected Behavior
According to the RISC-V Privileged Specification, `mstatus.SXL` is the effective XLEN for S-mode and must be read-only zero when S-mode is not implemented, and `mstatus.UXL` is the effective XLEN for U-mode and must be read-only zero when U-mode is not implemented. On RV64 systems, these fields should only report `XLEN_64` for privilege modes that are actually implemented.

## Actual Behavior
In the CSR register file logic (`csr_regfile.sv`), `SXL` and `UXL` are reported as `XLEN_64` on RV64 regardless of whether S-mode or U-mode are implemented. This means a machine-only configuration can still read both fields as non-zero, which violates the architectural definition of `mstatus`.

## Affected Function
The affected functionality is the CSR/mstatus reporting logic in the CSR register file, specifically the logic that constructs the architectural `mstatus` view for RV64 configurations.

## Trigger Condition
The bug is triggered when CVA6 is built without S-mode (`RVS=0`) and/or without U-mode (`RVU=0`) and software reads `mstatus`. The machine-only case where both modes are disabled is a direct reproducer: `SXL` and `UXL` should both read as 0, but they instead read as a valid XLEN encoding.

problem_statement: In Caliptra's KeyVault read client (`kv_read_client`), the status for a multi-beat read transaction can be overwritten by a later beat instead of preserving an earlier failure. If a KeyVault read stays active across multiple beats and one non-final beat reports a read error, a subsequent successful beat, including the final beat, can incorrectly make the overall transaction appear successful. `kv_read_client` is the block that returns KeyVault data to Caliptra hardware consumers. The expected behavior is that once any beat in a read transaction reports a KeyVault read failure, that failure remains latched for the rest of the transaction and the completed read reports failure rather than success.

problem_statement: In Caliptra's Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) engine, software can still rewrite the KeyVault private-key read-control register after an ECC signing operation has started. KeyVault is Caliptra's internal key storage interface used by crypto blocks to fetch protected key material. When ECC signing is configured to use a private key from a KeyVault entry, the selected entry must remain fixed for the entire signing operation. If software writes a different value to the ECC KeyVault private-key control register while the ECC engine is busy, that write should be ignored and the signature should still be generated from the key that was selected before the operation began. Instead, the active KeyVault private-key selection can change mid-operation, which changes the ECC signing result.

problem_statement: In Caliptra 2.0, the VeeR EL2 RISC-V core's AXI4-to-AHB bridge mishandles back-to-back read requests on the load/store path. If one read is followed immediately by another and the AHB-Lite slave deasserts HREADY while the second request is being presented, the bridge can change that second transfer from a valid AHB NONSEQ read to the wrong transfer type and can lose the low address bits of the buffered request. As a result, the second read can appear on AHB at an aligned or otherwise incorrect address instead of the requested address. The correct behavior is to keep the stalled second read as a valid NONSEQ transfer and preserve its exact requested address, including the low address bits, until the AHB slave accepts it.

resolved_issues.body:
This occurs due to the AHB signalling protocol. 
hreadyout is 0 for 1 cycle while hresp = 1. 
Current logic uses hready_i to clear the 'dv' signal or load a new request in from AHB, but that causes pending transactions to be resent on the component interface.

problem_statement: In Caliptra's `ahb_slv_sif` block, which bridges the AMBA Advanced High-performance Bus (AHB) to an internal client request interface, the downstream request-valid signal `dv` remains asserted for one extra clock after an outstanding transfer receives an error response. The bug is triggered when an AHB transfer has already been accepted, the internal client holds the request for at least one cycle, and then the client reports an error during the first AHB error-response cycle while the AHB bus is still not ready. The observed incorrect behavior is that `dv` stays high on that error cycle instead of clearing. The expected behavior is that as soon as the outstanding request completes with an error, `dv` must deassert in that same cycle and remain low until a new valid AHB transfer is accepted.

resolved_issues.body:
The problem happens when the arbiter gets the Read and Write transaction in the same clock cycle. The arbiter is supposed to prioritize Write over Read, however if both of them happen at the same time, the arbiter issues two writes (with the same data) to the underlying logic and the Read is lost.

This issue has been fixed in the i3c-core (which uses the same subordinate AXI arbiter) with https://github.com/chipsalliance/i3c-core/commit/676fc8ed5c38aa4aa61f07988c7dc5303bc03be1

prepare_script:
#!/bin/bash
set -e

BASE_SHA="d1a3be59fdadce8169398fd77acc717dc33d282c"

# Stage 1: checkout base_sha in a clean workspace.
cd /home/caliptra-rtl
git reset --hard
git clean -fdx

if ! git cat-file -e "${BASE_SHA}^{commit}" 2>/dev/null; then
  git fetch --depth=1 origin "${BASE_SHA}"
fi

git checkout "${BASE_SHA}"

# Stage 2: sync submodules to the checked-out commit.
git submodule sync --recursive || true
git submodule update --init --recursive || true

# Normalize the one CRLF source file touched by fix.patch so the runtime-mounted
# LF patch applies cleanly inside the harness.
perl -0pi -e 's/\r\n/\n/g' src/integration/rtl/caliptra_top.sv

# Stage 3: detect tool versions from the checked-out repo and align the environment.
verilator_version="v5.044"
riscv_version="v12.1.0"
workflow_file=".github/workflows/build-test-verilator.yml"

if [[ -f "$workflow_file" ]]; then
  detected_verilator="$(awk -F': ' '/^[[:space:]]+VERILATOR_VERSION:/ {gsub(/"/, "", $2); print $2; exit}' "$workflow_file")"
  detected_riscv="$(awk -F': ' '/^[[:space:]]+RISCV_VERSION:/ {gsub(/"/, "", $2); print $2; exit}' "$workflow_file")"
  if [[ -n "$detected_verilator" ]]; then
    verilator_version="$detected_verilator"
  fi
  if [[ -n "$detected_riscv" ]]; then
    riscv_version="$detected_riscv"
  fi
fi

echo "[INFO] Requested Verilator version: ${verilator_version}"
echo "[INFO] Requested RISC-V toolchain version: ${riscv_version}"

if ! command -v verilator >/dev/null 2>&1 || ! verilator --version | head -n1 | grep -q "${verilator_version#v}"; then
  /usr/local/bin/install-verilator-version "${verilator_version}"
fi

if ! command -v riscv64-unknown-elf-gcc >/dev/null 2>&1 || ! riscv64-unknown-elf-gcc --version | head -n1 | grep -q "${riscv_version#v}"; then
  /usr/local/bin/install-caliptra-riscv-toolchain "${riscv_version}"
fi

hash -r

# Stage 4: install minimal Python deps used by the open-source smoke/regression scripts.
python -m pip install -U pip setuptools wheel pyyaml
python -m pip show pyyaml >/dev/null

if [[ ! -f tools/scripts/Makefile ]]; then
  echo "[ERROR] tools/scripts/Makefile not found at ${BASE_SHA}"
  exit 1
fi

verilator --version | head -n1
riscv64-unknown-elf-gcc --version | head -n1
python --version
problem_statement: In Caliptra's AXI subordinate arbiter (`axi_sub_arb`), overlapping read and write traffic can be arbitrated incorrectly when a read request has already been selected but is still blocked by downstream backpressure. If a write request becomes valid in the same cycle that the downstream hold is released, the arbiter can switch to the write too early and the pending read can be lost. This affects the AXI block that merges read and write requests onto a shared downstream request interface. The expected behavior is testable: once a read or write beat has won arbitration, that winner must remain selected until the downstream interface actually accepts that beat; only after the accepted transfer completes may the arbiter apply its normal write-over-read priority to choose the next request. Under this trigger condition, the stalled read must complete first, and the write may be issued only afterward.

title: [RTL] Disable RV USER_MODE and SMEPMP
body:
Disable SMEPMP as it is not required for the baseline PMP feature.
PMP is enabled by default, per https://github.com/chipsalliance/Cores-VeeR-EL2/issues/258
SMEPMP is an extended feature that implicitly only applies when USER_MODE is enabled, which is not the use-case for Caliptra Core in 2.0.
Partially addresses #631

problem_statement: Caliptra Core 2.0 integrates a VeeR EL2 RISC-V core for firmware execution, and this configuration is intended to use only machine mode with baseline Physical Memory Protection (PMP), not the Smepmp extension. In the affected RISC-V PMP control path, PMP configuration writes still behave as if the Smepmp/user-mode feature set is present. As a result, if firmware clears pmpcfg0 and then writes the illegal baseline PMP permission encoding R=0 and W=1 into the low byte, for example by writing 0x02, the low byte is preserved as 0x02 on readback instead of being forced to a valid value. The expected behavior is that, in Caliptra's machine-mode-only baseline PMP configuration, unsupported Smepmp-specific behavior must not be exposed and an illegal pmpcfg permission encoding such as R=0/W=1 must read back as 0x00 after the write. This is triggered when firmware programs PMP CSRs in the Caliptra Core 2.0 RISC-V subsystem and writes that illegal permission combination into a pmpcfg entry.
