resolved_issues.title: [ entropy_src rtl, dv ] Do not clear entropy_src statistics on disable
resolved_issues.body:
The health check statistics registers (watermarks, test failure counts, alert counts etc.) have all proven to be essential tools for verification.    In DV these registers are read and scoreboarded
- At the end of every simulation, and
- Every time an alert occurs.
However these checks are made more complicated by the fact that these registers are cleared every time the IP is disabled.  Ideally DV would be able to disable the DUT, check the statistics.  This would allow the testbench to take a clean snapshot of the health check data.

However since these registers are cleared once the enable register is set to `MuBi4False` this forced the test bench to read these stats while the DUT is still collecting data.
  
If the RNG test runs long enough (about 2ms) eventually the testbench will encounter a scenario where the test tries to read a register as it is being updated this leads to scenarios such as in the following UVM error example:

```
UVM_WARNING @ 2534116459 ps: (uvm_reg_field.svh:1186) [RegModel] Trying to predict value of field 'markov_hi_total_fails' while register 'entropy_src_reg_block.markov_hi_total_fails' is being accessed
UVM_FATAL @ 2534116459 ps: (entropy_src_scoreboard.sv:324) [uvm_test_top.env.scoreboard] Check failed (total_fail_field.predict(.value(fail_total), .kind(UVM_PREDICT_DIRECT)))
```

This issue requests that the following registers not be cleared on disable, rather the clear event should be delayed to just before the following enable event: 
- repcnt_hi_watermarks
- repcnts_hi_watermarks
- adaptp_hi_watermarks
- adaptp_lo_watermarks
- extht_hi_watermarks
- extht_lo_watermarks
- bucket_hi_watermarks
- markov_hi_watermarks
- markov_lo_watermarks
- repcnt_total_fails
- repcnts_total_fails
- adaptp_hi_total_fails
- adaptp_lo_total_fails
- bucket_total_fails
- markov_hi_total_fails
- markov_lo_total_fails
- extht_hi_total_fails
- extht_lo_total_fails
- alert_summary_fail_counts
- alert_fail_counts
- extht_fail_counts

#!/bin/bash
cd /home/opentitan || exit 1

source /etc/opentitan_tools_path.sh >/dev/null 2>&1 || true

set +e
timeout 1800 ./util/dvsim/dvsim.py hw/ip/entropy_src/dv/entropy_src_sim_cfg.hjson \
  -i entropy_src_rng \
  -t vcs \
  --fixed-seed 1 \
  --scratch-root /home/opentitan/.tb_entropy_src_rng_repro \
  --local \
  --purge \
  --no-rerun \
  -v l
rc=$?
set -e

echo "HWE_BENCH_RESULTS_START"
if [ "$rc" -eq 0 ]; then
  echo "TEST: entropy_src_rng_disable_stats ... PASS"
else
  echo "TEST: entropy_src_rng_disable_stats ... FAIL"
fi
echo "HWE_BENCH_RESULTS_END"

exit "$rc"
problem_statement:
## Description
OpenTitan's Entropy Source IP records health-test results in read-only control/status registers (CSRs) so firmware and design verification (DV) can inspect the outcome of a run after collection stops. These statistics include watermark registers, total failure counters, and alert-related failure counters. The bug is that disabling the Entropy Source immediately destroys the accumulated statistics.

## Affected Function
The affected functionality is retention of Entropy Source health-test statistics in CSRs, including `repcnt_hi_watermarks`, `repcnts_hi_watermarks`, `adaptp_hi_watermarks`, `adaptp_lo_watermarks`, `extht_hi_watermarks`, `extht_lo_watermarks`, `bucket_hi_watermarks`, `markov_hi_watermarks`, `markov_lo_watermarks`, the corresponding `*_total_fails` counters, `alert_summary_fail_counts`, `alert_fail_counts`, and `extht_fail_counts`.

## Expected Behavior
After the Entropy Source is disabled, these statistics CSRs should stop changing but must continue to hold the values accumulated during the completed run so software or DV can read a clean, stable snapshot. The listed registers should be cleared only when a new Entropy Source run starts because the IP is enabled again, not when the current run is disabled.

## Actual Behavior
When the main enable is turned off, the Entropy Source clears the accumulated health-test statistics immediately. This removes the post-run snapshot needed for verification and firmware analysis, so the only remaining option is to read the statistics while the block is still active and the counters or watermarks may still be updating. In long-running random-number-generator health-test simulations, that can produce scoreboard mismatches when a statistics CSR is read around the same time it changes.

## Trigger Condition
The bug appears when the Entropy Source has been enabled long enough to accumulate health-test statistics and is then disabled before those statistics are read. It is especially exposed in random-number-generator mode tests that disable the block before checking the statistics CSRs at the end of collection.

resolved_issues.title: [sw, dif, aes] The AES DIF is mixing up MODE and OPERATION

problem_statement:
OpenTitan's AES Device Interface Function (DIF) incorrectly translates a `dif_aes_transaction_t` into the shadowed AES control register (`AES_CTRL_SHADOWED`). The affected functionality is the AES DIF transaction setup path that programs the AES control fields before a transaction starts.

The expected behavior is that the control register fields are derived directly and independently from the transaction description. In particular, the MODE field must come from `transaction.mode`, and the OPERATION field must come from `transaction.operation`. A request for Cipher Block Chaining (CBC) decryption must therefore program CBC in the MODE field and decryption in the OPERATION field. Software must be able to request non-Electronic Codebook (non-ECB) modes through the transaction itself rather than through a separate mode-selection path.

The observed behavior is that these control fields are mixed up when the AES DIF prepares the register value. The transaction's `mode` is not used correctly to drive the MODE field, and the OPERATION field can be chosen using the wrong transaction field. As a result, the value written to `AES_CTRL_SHADOWED` can differ from the requested transaction, so non-ECB requests and decrypt requests can be configured incorrectly.

This bug is triggered when software starts an AES transaction through the AES DIF and relies on the transaction structure as the source of truth for configuration. A concrete failing case is a CBC decryption request: after the DIF programs `AES_CTRL_SHADOWED`, the MODE and OPERATION fields may not match the CBC-decrypt transaction that software requested.

problem_statement:
## Description
The KMAC (Keccak Message Authentication Code) IP exposes an entropy refresh threshold that controls after how many hash operations the block should request a new entropy seed from the EDN (Entropy Distribution Network). This threshold is configuration state and is intended to be protected by shadowed control and status register (CSR) semantics.

## Expected Behavior
The KMAC entropy refresh threshold CSR must behave as a shadowed register. After the first write of an update sequence, software should still read back the previously committed threshold value. The new threshold should become visible only after a second matching write completes the shadowed update.

## Actual Behavior
In the affected implementation, the entropy refresh threshold behaves like a normal writable CSR field instead of a shadowed one. After a single write, software can immediately read back the new threshold value even though the confirming second write has not occurred.

## Affected Function
This affects the KMAC CSR block's entropy refresh threshold configuration register, which controls the threshold used for requesting fresh entropy from the EDN.

## Trigger Condition
The bug appears when firmware updates the entropy refresh threshold while configuration writes are enabled but stops after the first write of the shadowed-register sequence. A read performed after that first write returns the new value instead of the previously committed threshold.

problem_statement:
## Description
The bug is in the OpenTitan Key Manager (`keymgr`) hardware block's alert interface. `keymgr` exposes two named alerts: the recoverable operation alert `recov_operation_err` and the fatal fault alert `fatal_fault_err`. These names are assigned to the wrong alert output indexes, so the named alert order does not match the physical alert outputs.

## Expected Behavior
`recov_operation_err` must be connected to the first `keymgr` alert output (alert index 0), and `fatal_fault_err` must be connected to the second `keymgr` alert output (alert index 1). When software writes the `recov_operation_err` bit in the `ALERT_TEST` register, only the recovery alert output should assert and the fatal alert output must remain deasserted.

## Actual Behavior
The two `keymgr` alert indexes are reversed. Forcing `recov_operation_err` through the `ALERT_TEST` register can assert alert index 1, which is the fatal alert output, while alert index 0 does not assert.

## Affected Function
The affected functionality is the `keymgr` alert definition and wiring, including the mapping between the named alerts in the register interface and the module's two alert outputs.

## Trigger Condition
The mismatch is observable when software forces the recovery alert by setting the `recov_operation_err` bit in the `ALERT_TEST` register.

fi

# Stage 3: install Python dependencies from the checked-out repo.
if [[ -f python-requirements.txt ]]; then
  echo "[INFO] Installing Python deps from python-requirements.txt"
  python -m pip install -U pip "setuptools<66.0.0"

  python -m pip install -r "${PREP_ROOT}/python-requirements.txt" --no-warn-script-location
else

# Stage 4: install the toolchain and Verible outside the repo so runtime git clean does not remove them.

problem_statement:
## Description
In OpenTitan Key Manager (`keymgr`), the control logic retains an internal working key in storage between commands. That retained working-key storage is not protected with error-correcting code (ECC). If a storage fault flips a bit in the retained working key while `keymgr` is idle, the corruption is not detected.

## Expected Behavior
The retained working-key storage in `keymgr` should be protected with ECC while the key is stored between operations. If the stored working key is corrupted, even when no new Key Manager command is running, `keymgr` must raise a fatal fault alert and transition its working state to `Invalid`.

## Actual Behavior
A bit flip in the retained working key while `keymgr` is idle can leave `keymgr` in a non-`Invalid` working state without raising a fatal fault alert.

resolved_issues.title: [spi_device] Write enable (WREN) and write disable (WRDI) should be handled in hardware
resolved_issues.body:
The write enable command (WREN, 0x06) sets the write enable latch (WEL) bit, while the write disable command (WRDI, 0x04) clears it. The host sends WREN every time before "writing" to the device, e.g. before chip/sector erase or page program. Since handling this in software would introduce additional latency; WREN & WRDI commands should be handled in hardware.

cc @cfrantz @a-will

    check_rw_csr("cmd_info_wrdi", 32'h8000_0004);

endclass

problem_statement:
## Description
The OpenTitan SPI Device IP, when operating in flash mode, lacks dedicated command-info Control and Status Registers (CSRs) for the standard SPI flash Write Enable (WREN, opcode 0x06) and Write Disable (WRDI, opcode 0x04) commands. These commands control the write enable latch (WEL) and are issued by an external SPI flash master before program or erase operations, so they are part of the flash command path that hardware must recognize without depending on firmware latency.

## Expected Behavior
The SPI Device flash command interface should expose dedicated software-visible command-info CSRs for WREN and WRDI. Software should be able to program and read back the opcode definitions for these two commands through the register interface, so WREN and WRDI are represented in the flash-mode command-info CSR map in the same way as the other special flash commands.

## Actual Behavior
In the affected implementation, the SPI Device register model has no dedicated command-info CSRs for WREN or WRDI. Software cannot program or read back per-command entries for these opcodes, leaving the flash-mode command-info interface incomplete for these two standard commands.

## Trigger Condition
The problem appears when the SPI Device IP is used in flash mode and software or verification expects dedicated register entries for WREN and WRDI, especially in flows where an external SPI flash master issues WREN or WRDI before a write, page-program, or erase operation.

problem_statement:
## Description
In the OpenTitan Power Manager (`pwrmgr`) IP, a transient glitch on the main power domain (`main_pd`) after the block has reached normal active operation already pushes the power manager into its reset-preparation flow, but the event is not fully reported as a fault.

## Expected Behavior
If `pwrmgr` detects an unexpected drop and recovery of the `main_pd` power-good signal while the system is active, it should enter the main-power reset-preparation sequence, assert the `pwrmgr` alert, and latch a software-readable `main_pd` glitch indication in the fault-status control/status register (CSR).

## Actual Behavior
The transient `main_pd` glitch still drives `pwrmgr` into reset preparation, but `pwrmgr` does not raise the alert for this case and does not latch a dedicated `main_pd` glitch fault indication for software.

## Affected Function
The affected logic is the OpenTitan Power Manager (`pwrmgr`) fault-reporting path for main power-domain glitches, specifically the logic that generates alerts and records fault causes when the main-power reset path is entered.

## Trigger Condition
This occurs when the `main_pd` power-good signal briefly drops and then returns after `pwrmgr` has reached its normal active state.

- fixes #12167

The host region decoding forgot to include the 'en' bit, causing
host read attributes to sometimes differ from the controller attributes.

Signed-off-by: Timothy Chen <timothytim@google.com>

resolved_issues.title: [flash_ctrl] host direct access attribute decoding error
resolved_issues.body:
host direct access into flash do not currently receive the same attributes as flash controller accesses.
This is because the host region decode forgets to incorporate the "EN" bit while the flash controller does.

This is an error on the host region decoding and leads to test failures in `flash_ctrl_host_dir_rd`.

problem_statement:
## Description
In the OpenTitan flash controller IP (`flash_ctrl`), the host interface direct-read path for the flash data partition can decode memory-protection region attributes differently from controller-initiated flash accesses. The original issue reports that the host region decode does not incorporate the region enable (`EN`) bit, so a host direct read can use attributes from a region that is not actually enabled.

## Expected Behavior
For any flash data-partition address, the host interface direct-read path and the controller path must use the same effective access attributes. If an address falls inside the range of a memory-protection region whose `EN` bit is not active, that region must not affect the access; the host direct read must behave as if the disabled region were absent, matching the controller's view of the same address. In particular, in a configuration where scrambling is enabled for the effective access, a word programmed and then read back through the controller must match the data returned by a host direct read of that same word.

## Actual Behavior
A host direct read can apply attributes from a memory-protection region based only on the address range, even when that region is disabled. As a result, the data returned by a host direct read can differ from the data returned by a controller read of the same programmed flash word.

## Trigger Condition
This occurs when a host interface direct read targets a flash data-partition address that lies within the range of a configured memory-protection region whose `EN` bit is not active. The regression exposes the bug when that location is then compared between the controller read path and the host direct-read path in a scramble-enabled configuration.

resolved_issues.title: [spi_device] Write enable (WREN) and write disable (WRDI) should be handled in hardware
resolved_issues.body:
The write enable command (WREN, 0x06) sets the write enable latch (WEL) bit, while the write disable command (WRDI, 0x04) clears it. The host sends WREN every time before "writing" to the device, e.g. before chip/sector erase or page program. Since handling this in software would introduce additional latency; WREN & WRDI commands should be handled in hardware.

cc @cfrantz @a-will

problem_statement:
## Description
OpenTitan's SPI Device hardware block can act as an SPI flash target. In the `silicon_creator` boot firmware initialization path, `spi_device_init()` does not enable hardware handling of the standard SPI flash Write Enable (WREN, 0x06) and Write Disable (WRDI, 0x04) commands. That leaves this initialization path without the expected hardware-managed write-enable latch behavior.

## Expected Behavior
After `spi_device_init()` configures the SPI Device for flash-style operation, WREN must be recognized in hardware and set the write enable latch (WEL) bit in the status register, while WRDI must be recognized in hardware and clear the same WEL bit. An external SPI host that issues Read Status (0x05) after WREN should observe WEL asserted, and the same status read after WRDI should observe WEL deasserted, without requiring software handling of those commands.

## Actual Behavior
With the current `spi_device_init()` configuration, WREN and WRDI are not enabled as hardware-handled flash commands for this boot-firmware path. As a result, an external SPI host cannot rely on the normal WREN -> Read Status -> WRDI -> Read Status sequence to drive the WEL bit through the expected set and clear transitions.

## Affected Module
The affected area is the `silicon_creator` boot firmware's SPI Device initialization path, specifically the SPI Device flash-command configuration performed by `spi_device_init()`.

## Trigger Condition
The bug is triggered when the SPI Device has been initialized by `spi_device_init()` for flash-style operation and an external SPI host sends WREN or WRDI, then reads status to check the WEL state.

## Description
In OpenTitan, the silicon_creator boot firmware initializes the SPI Device peripheral's JEDEC device-identification register in `spi_device_init()`. The Life Cycle Controller (LC_CTRL) provides the hardware revision as separate chip-generation and chip-revision values, and that revision information is intended to populate the SPI Device JEDEC ID used for bootstrap and reporting.

## Expected Behavior
After `spi_device_init()` completes, the SPI Device JEDEC ID register must encode the current LC_CTRL hardware revision in its `CHIP_GEN` and `CHIP_REV` fields. Because those JEDEC fields are narrower than the LC_CTRL hardware-revision fields, each JEDEC field should contain the least-significant bits of the corresponding LC_CTRL value that fit in the field.

## Actual Behavior
`spi_device_init()` leaves the JEDEC `CHIP_GEN` and `CHIP_REV` fields at zero instead of deriving them from LC_CTRL. When LC_CTRL reports non-zero hardware-revision bits, software that reads the SPI Device JEDEC ID register sees revision fields that do not match the device's hardware revision.

## Affected Module
This bug affects the silicon_creator SPI Device initialization path, specifically the JEDEC ID setup for the SPI Device peripheral and its interaction with the Life Cycle Controller (LC_CTRL) hardware-revision register.

## Trigger Condition
The mismatch is observable whenever `spi_device_init()` runs on hardware or simulation where the LC_CTRL hardware revision contains non-zero bits within the width of the JEDEC `CHIP_GEN` or `CHIP_REV` fields. Reading the SPI Device JEDEC ID register after initialization then returns zero in one or both revision fields instead of the truncated LC_CTRL hardware revision.

title: [flash_ctrl/prim] Flash interrupt usability and modeling updates
body:
- Address some usability issues identified in https://github.com/lowRISC/opentitan/pull/12834

- Read level interrupt is intended to trigger
  when the flash read deposits more than N number of
  entries into the FIFO. Therefore trigger only
  when there has been a deposit and not on withdrawals.

- Similarly, program level interrupt is intended to
  trigger when the flash withdraws more than N number
  of entries from the FIFO.  Therefore trigger only
  when there has been a withdrawwl, and not on
  deposits.

- Added a couple of parameters that could be employed by a user
  to change the model read/program/erase latency

- This is especially useful for interrupt tests, as the default
  access latencies for read are too small to make interrupts
  useable.

commits.message:
[flash_ctrl/prim_flash] Add parameters to tweak module latency

- Added a couple of parameters that could be employed by a user
  to change the model read/program/erase latency

- This is especially useful for interrupt tests, as the default
  access latencies for read are too small to make interrupts
  useable.

Signed-off-by: Timothy Chen <timothytim@google.com>

[flash_ctrl] Change level interrupt triggering condition

- Address some usability issues identified in #12834

- Read level interrupt is intended to trigger
  when the flash read deposits more than N number of
  entries into the FIFO. Therefore trigger only
  when there has been a deposit and not on withdrawals.

- Similarly, program level interrupt is intended to
  trigger when the flash withdraws more than N number
  of entries from the FIFO.  Therefore trigger only
  when there has been a withdrawwl, and not on
  deposits.

Signed-off-by: Timothy Chen <timothytim@google.com>

prepare_script:
#!/bin/bash
set -e

# Stage 1: checkout base_sha in a clean workspace (+submodules)
cd /home/opentitan
git reset --hard
git clean -fdx
git checkout 19a31959ad5e60ad1deaf1cfa5087cc183d24948
git submodule update --init --recursive

# Stage 2: install repository apt dependencies
export DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive
if [[ -f apt-requirements.txt ]]; then
  cp apt-requirements.txt /tmp/opentitan-apt-requirements.txt
  sed -i -e '/^$/d' -e '/^#/d' -e 's/#.*//' /tmp/opentitan-apt-requirements.txt
  if [[ -s /tmp/opentitan-apt-requirements.txt ]]; then
    apt-get update
    xargs -r apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends < /tmp/opentitan-apt-requirements.txt
    rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
  fi
  rm -f /tmp/opentitan-apt-requirements.txt
fi

# Stage 3: install Python dependencies required by dvsim / FuseSoC
python -m pip install -U pip "setuptools<66.0.0"
grep -vE '^(types-dataclasses|types-pkg_resources)$' python-requirements.txt \
  > /tmp/opentitan-python-requirements.txt
python -m pip install -r /tmp/opentitan-python-requirements.txt --no-warn-script-location
rm -f /tmp/opentitan-python-requirements.txt

# Stage 4: this VCS-only flash_ctrl DV flow does not require downloading the
# legacy Verible release encoded in this commit's Dockerfile. Keep optional tool
# directories on PATH if they already exist.
cat > /etc/opentitan_tools_path.sh <<'EOF'
for d in /tools/riscv/bin /tools/verible/bin; do
  if [ -d "$d" ]; then
    export PATH="$d:$PATH"
  fi
done
true
EOF
if ! grep -q "/etc/opentitan_tools_path.sh" /etc/opentitan_bash_env; then
  echo "source /etc/opentitan_tools_path.sh" >> /etc/opentitan_bash_env
fi
source /etc/opentitan_tools_path.sh

python -m pip show edalize fusesoc hjson >/dev/null
problem_statement:
## Description
In the OpenTitan Flash Controller IP, the program FIFO level interrupt (`prog_lvl`) is generated from the current `prog_fifo` depth without distinguishing whether that depth changed because software deposited data or because an active flash program operation withdrew data. As a result, `prog_lvl` can assert immediately after software writes program words into `prog_fifo`, creating a false indication that the controller is ready for a refill.

## Expected Behavior
`prog_lvl` is a refill interrupt for the program FIFO. It should assert only after a flash program operation withdraws entries from `prog_fifo` and the remaining FIFO depth reaches the configured program FIFO interrupt threshold. Software writes that deposit data into `prog_fifo` must not assert `prog_lvl`.

## Actual Behavior
During an in-progress flash program transaction, `prog_lvl` can assert as soon as software writes data into `prog_fifo`, before the controller has consumed any queued program word.

## Trigger Conditions
This appears when a flash program operation is already running and the program FIFO interrupt threshold is configured to a low value such as 1 entry. In that state, writing program words into `prog_fifo` can incorrectly raise `prog_lvl` even though no withdrawal-based refill condition has occurred.

## Affected Function
The affected logic is the OpenTitan Flash Controller IP's program FIFO level interrupt generation for `prog_lvl`.

resolved_issues.body:
This issue is similar to #10134, in that it involves recoverable alerts that are firing continuously.  In this case it is the 11 different `*_FIELD_ALERTS` which are designed to check whether a bad MuBi has been received.   Once a bad MuBi has been written the alert fires continuously until the bad MuBi has been corrected.

This was not caught previously because the up to now the only sequence that performed such tests did not use scoreboarding.  However now that this class alert events is being added to the scoreboard however, this is causing troubles with verification.  The alerts are firing continuously and do not stop until the bad register has been corrected.  However, there is no time for the sequence to identify the problem before the alert refires. problem_statement:
## Description
The affected module is the OpenTitan Entropy Source IP, specifically the shared recoverable alert output (`recov_alert`) associated with the Entropy Source `*_FIELD_ALERTS` checks. These checks detect invalid MuBi (multi-bit boolean) encodings written into MuBi-protected control fields.

## Expected Behavior
If software writes an invalid MuBi value to a protected Entropy Source control field, the corresponding `*_FIELD_ALERTS` status bit should latch and `recov_alert` should be emitted as a single alert pulse for that event. After the alert receiver completes the alert handshake, `recov_alert` should return low even if the invalid register value is still present, so one bad programmed state does not immediately retrigger additional recoverable alerts. This behavior must hold for firmware-controlled MuBi fields such as `FIPS_ENABLE`.

## Actual Behavior
`recov_alert` behaves as a level derived from the latched field-alert condition instead of as a pulse. After an invalid MuBi value is written, the alert keeps re-firing or staying asserted until software corrects the bad register value, so a single field-validation failure produces repeated recoverable alerts.

## Trigger Condition
The bug is triggered by programming an invalid MuBi encoding into a MuBi-protected Entropy Source control field that raises a `*_FIELD_ALERTS` condition, including the `FIPS_ENABLE` case.

problem_statement:
## Description
In the OpenTitan `spi_device` IP, the flash-mode `LAST_READ_ADDR` control/status register (CSR) does not reliably report the address of the last byte that the SPI host read from the read buffer. Instead, the register can retain an address value that was latched earlier during read-command processing, before the transaction has finished returning data.

## Expected Behavior
After a flash-mode read-buffer transaction completes, `LAST_READ_ADDR` must equal the host-visible address of the final byte returned to the SPI host from the read buffer. If a read command starts at address `A` and returns `N` bytes from the read buffer, software should observe `LAST_READ_ADDR = A + N - 1` after the transaction.

## Actual Behavior
`LAST_READ_ADDR` reflects the earlier latched read-command address state rather than the final byte address that was actually returned. In multi-byte read-buffer transactions, software can therefore observe the starting command address instead of the address of the last byte delivered to the host.

## Affected Function
This affects the `spi_device` flash-mode read-command path, specifically the logic that updates the `LAST_READ_ADDR` CSR for read-buffer transactions. The linked issue history also ties this bug to the same address-latching path used when distinguishing read-buffer accesses from mailbox-region accesses.

## Trigger Condition
The bug appears when the SPI host performs a flash-mode read that returns data from the read buffer, especially when more than one data byte is returned and software inspects `LAST_READ_ADDR` after the transaction.

problem_statement:
## Description
The bug is in the OTP Controller (One-Time Programmable controller) device interface functions (DIFs) that manage runtime check locks and software-partition read locks. The DIF code confuses the configuration lock (`CHECK_REGWEN`) with the check-trigger lock (`CHECK_TRIGGER_REGWEN`), and it still handles several lock-enable bits as if writing `1` would clear them even though the current hardware contract requires write-0-to-clear behavior.

## Expected Behavior
`CHECK_REGWEN` and `CHECK_TRIGGER_REGWEN` protect different OTP Controller operations and must be checked independently. Locking `CHECK_REGWEN` should block only runtime check configuration; runtime integrity and consistency checks should remain available until `CHECK_TRIGGER_REGWEN` is locked. When software requests any of these locks, the DIF must clear the relevant enable bit by writing `0`, because those lock bits use write-0-to-clear semantics. The same rule applies to read-lock registers for software partitions. In addition, a software-partition read-lock request must respect `DIRECT_ACCESS_REGWEN`: if the direct access interface (DAI) is busy and that write-enable bit is cleared, the DIF must return `kDifUnavailable` instead of issuing the lock write.

## Actual Behavior
The DIF checks the wrong lock register before starting integrity or consistency checks, so it can treat the trigger path as locked when only configuration was locked. It also writes the wrong value when trying to clear lock-enable bits, so configuration locks or software-partition read locks may not actually take effect. For software-partition read locks, the DIF can also proceed while the DAI is busy even though the hardware interface is not writable.

## Affected Area
OTP Controller DIF lock handling for runtime check configuration, runtime integrity and consistency check triggering, and software-partition read locks.

## Trigger Conditions
This appears when software exercises the OTP lock APIs after the controller moved to write-0-to-clear register-write-enable behavior, especially when integrity or consistency checks depend on `CHECK_TRIGGER_REGWEN` while `CHECK_REGWEN` is in a different state, or when a software-partition read lock is requested while `DIRECT_ACCESS_REGWEN` is low because the DAI is busy.

problem_statement:
## Description
The HMAC (Hash-based Message Authentication Code) hardware IP block in OpenTitan exposes a single alert output. At the top-level system integration, that alert is treated as a fatal alert source, but the HMAC alert sender does not classify its only alert as fatal. As a result, the HMAC alert behaves like a recoverable alert even though the rest of the system expects fatal-alert behavior.

## Expected Behavior
HMAC's single alert output must use fatal-alert semantics. After an HMAC alert has been observed, acknowledging the corresponding alert cause while the HMAC clock is gated off must not permanently retire the condition. When the HMAC clock is enabled again, the OpenTitan alert handler should observe the HMAC alert cause asserted again.

## Actual Behavior
The initial HMAC alert can be observed, but if the HMAC clock is disabled before the alert cause is acknowledged, the cause clears on acknowledge and remains cleared after the clock is restored. This is recoverable-alert behavior, not fatal-alert behavior.

## Affected Module
The bug is in the HMAC IP's single alert output path, specifically the severity classification passed to the alert sender that reports HMAC faults to the OpenTitan alert handler.

## Trigger Conditions
The issue appears when an HMAC alert is triggered, the HMAC peripheral clock is turned off during alert handling, the alert cause is acknowledged while that clock is off, and the clock is later turned back on.

problem_statement:
## Description
In the Entropy Distribution Network (EDN) IP, the fatal error reporting interface is inconsistent for the output first-in, first-out (FIFO) path. The issue report notes that the `ERR_CODE` register describes bits `[19:2]` as reserved, but writing value `2` to `ERR_CODE_TEST` can still trigger a fatal alert. Bit 2 is associated with the output FIFO error source, so the software-visible status map does not match the error-injection map.

## Expected Behavior
`ERR_CODE_TEST` and `ERR_CODE` should use the same error-bit mapping. When software writes `2` to `ERR_CODE_TEST`, the EDN should report the corresponding fatal error source in `ERR_CODE[2]` instead of treating bit 2 as reserved. This makes the alert source identifiable to firmware.

## Actual Behavior
Writing `2` to `ERR_CODE_TEST` can trigger the fatal alert path, but `ERR_CODE[2]` is not exposed as a defined output FIFO error status bit. Software can therefore observe a fatal EDN failure without a matching `ERR_CODE` indication for that source.

## Affected Function
The affected functionality is EDN fatal error status and error-injection handling for the output FIFO path, specifically the mapping between the `ERR_CODE_TEST` and `ERR_CODE` registers.

## Trigger Condition
The inconsistency is observable when software writes value `2` to the EDN `ERR_CODE_TEST` register to inject the output FIFO fatal error condition.

python3 - <<'PY'
from pathlib import Path

root = Path("/home/opentitan")

seq = root / "hw/ip/flash_ctrl/dv/env/seq_lib/flash_ctrl_init_status_vseq.sv"
seq.write_text(
    """// Copyright lowRISC contributors.
// Licensed under the Apache License, Version 2.0, see LICENSE for details.
// SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0

class flash_ctrl_init_status_vseq extends flash_ctrl_base_vseq;
  `uvm_object_utils(flash_ctrl_init_status_vseq)
  `uvm_object_new

  task body();
    uvm_reg_data_t status;
    bit initialized;

    csr_spinwait(.ptr(ral.status.init_wip), .exp_data(1'b0));
    cfg.clk_rst_vif.wait_clks(5);
    csr_rd(.ptr(ral.status), .value(status));
    initialized = (status >> 5) & 1'b1;

    `uvm_info(`gfn, $sformatf("flash status after init: 0x%0h", status), UVM_MEDIUM)
    if (status[4]) begin
      `uvm_fatal(`gfn, $sformatf("init_wip should be 0 after initialization, got status=0x%0h",

    if (!initialized) begin

                                 status))
    end
  endtask : body
endclass : flash_ctrl_init_status_vseq
"""
)

def insert_once(path: Path, anchor: str, addition: str) -> None:
    text = path.read_text()

problem_statement:
## Description
The OpenTitan flash controller (`flash_ctrl`) `STATUS` Control and Status Register (CSR) indicates whether flash initialization is busy, but it does not indicate whether flash initialization has completed. This makes it possible for software to confuse a controller that has finished initializing and is now idle with a controller that has not initialized at all.

## Expected Behavior
Once flash initialization completes, the `STATUS` CSR must let firmware distinguish two states: "initialization still in progress" and "initialization completed." In particular, when initialization has finished and the controller is idle, the status must show both that initialization is no longer busy and that initialization has completed.

## Actual Behavior
The current `STATUS` CSR only reports whether initialization is busy. After the busy indication clears, software cannot tell whether initialization completed successfully or whether the controller is simply not initialized, because both cases appear as not busy.

## Affected Function
The affected functionality is the flash controller (`flash_ctrl`) software-visible initialization status reporting through the `STATUS` CSR.

## Trigger Condition
This bug is exposed when firmware polls the flash controller `STATUS` CSR as the controller transitions from initialization-in-progress to the idle post-initialization state.

title: [hmac,dv/rtl] Implement DV checks for new digest sizes/key lengths
body:
This PR implements scoreboard checks for the new HMAC digest sizes and key lengths for normal operation and whenever secure wiping is triggered.  For ease of DV checks and consistency across configuration changes where previous digests remain held in CSRs until HMAC starts a new operation, this PR also removes the clearing of redundant digest values for the smaller digest sizes in the RTL. It also updates the documentation to clarify that SW should only read the relevant digest CSRs for the digest size configured - @ballifatih (only read digests 0..7 for SHA-2 256 and digests 0..11 for SHA-2 384, i.e., do not assume the redundant digest values in these sizes will be all-zero.)

This should also fix the failing hmac_wipe_secret test (https://github.com/lowRISC/opentitan/issues/23053) and close other pending DV TODOS.

problem_statement:
## Description
The HMAC (Hash-based Message Authentication Code) IP exposes the current digest through `DIGEST_0`..`DIGEST_15` control/status registers (CSRs), and those registers can continue to hold the previous digest until a new hash operation starts. In secure-wipe flows and in digest reads performed after changing the HMAC configuration, readback for SHA-2 384 and SHA-2 512 is not handled consistently with this retained-digest behavior. Smaller-digest layouts are still treated as if the unused DIGEST words must always read back as zero, which leads to digest mismatches when a retained or wiped digest is read.

## Expected Behavior
Digest CSR readback must be interpreted according to the digest size that produced the digest currently visible in the registers: SHA-2 256 uses `DIGEST_0`..`DIGEST_7`, SHA-2 384 uses `DIGEST_0`..`DIGEST_11`, and SHA-2 512 uses `DIGEST_0`..`DIGEST_15`. For SHA-2 256 and SHA-2 384, the remaining DIGEST words are not part of the digest and must not be required to read as zero. If `wipe_secret` is triggered, any digest still visible in the DIGEST CSRs must be treated as corrupted regardless of digest size or HMAC key length.

## Affected Function
The affected functionality is the HMAC IP DIGEST CSR readback path, including retained-digest handling across configuration changes and secret-wipe behavior for SHA-2 256, SHA-2 384, and SHA-2 512 operation.

## Trigger Condition
This is triggered when software or verification reads the DIGEST CSRs after a SHA-2 384 or SHA-2 512 operation, after changing digest size or HMAC key length while the previous digest is still retained, or after asserting `wipe_secret` before that retained or current digest is replaced by a new operation.

resolved_issues.title: [hmac/dv] CSR read check commented out in scoreboard
resolved_issues.body:
### Description

In the HMAC SB, there is condition on "do_read_check" to enable data comparison. But this is commented out since mid-February.

problem_statement:
OpenTitan's HMAC (Hash-based Message Authentication Code) IP has a synchronization problem in the SHA-384/SHA-512 status-reporting path. CSR (Control and Status Register) read checking in the HMAC DV (design verification) scoreboard had been disabled because, in these digest modes, reads of the software-visible `STATUS` register can stop matching the scoreboard's expected view while a message is being consumed from `MSG_FIFO`. The digest computation itself is not reported as incorrect; the mismatch is in the visible progress and status behavior during the operation.

Expected behavior: when the HMAC IP runs in the SHA-384/SHA-512 path, `STATUS` must continue to reflect the engine's real progress, including FIFO depth / empty state and idle-versus-busy state, so CSR read checking can remain enabled. In particular, during a SHA-512 operation on a full 1024-bit message block, repeated `STATUS` polls while the block is being loaded and processed should stay consistent with the actual message-consumption state until completion.

Affected module: the HMAC IP's SHA-384/SHA-512 message-loading and `STATUS` reporting path, together with the HMAC DV scoreboard logic that predicts `STATUS` reads for these digest sizes.

Trigger condition: start a SHA-512 hash, write a full 1024-bit message block into the HMAC message FIFO, and poll `STATUS` while the block is being consumed and processed. Under this condition, the expected and observed `STATUS` values can fall out of sync, which is why CSR read checking had been commented out for this path.

title: [hmac] Block the msg fifo request with packer ready
body:
This is follow-up PR for #683

Problem:

    In #683, the design unguarded msg_fifo_gnt signal from
    `fifo_wready`. It only needs to see `packer_ready`. This results
    unintended request acceptance as `msg_write` is also gated by
    `fifo_wready`.

What happend with the problem is, when the MSG_FIFO is full, it
de-asserts `fifo_wready`. At this time, `prim_packer` has still enough
room to accept one more request. It doesn't drop `packer_ready`
(`prim_packer.ready_o`) yet. So `msg_fifo_gnt` can be high whenever the
request comes. That request should've come to `prim_packer`, which
didn't happen due to the `msg_write` is gated by `fifo_wready`.

Resolution:

    `msg_write` is now gated by `packer_ready` not `fifo_wready`.

I've tested hmac_back_pressure test with modified design. It still
fails. But the failure isn't due to the modified design but the
scoreboard assumes getting the fifo_full status which cannot be happen
as the request was back-pressured and accepted after fifo_full condition
is resolved.

Cindy has a fix PR for this issue.

commits.message:
[hmac] Block the msg fifo request with packer ready

This is follow-up PR for #683

Problem 1:

    In #683, the design unguarded msg_fifo_gnt signal from
    `fifo_wready`. It only needs to see `packer_ready`. This results
    unintended request acceptance as `msg_write` is also gated by
    `fifo_wready`.

What happend with the problem is, when the MSG_FIFO is full, it
de-asserts `fifo_wready`. At this time, `prim_packer` has still enough
room to accept one more request. It doesn't drop `packer_ready`
(`prim_packer.ready_o`) yet. So `msg_fifo_gnt` can be high whenever the
request comes. That request should've come to `prim_packer`, which
didn't happen due to the `msg_write` is gated by `fifo_wready`.

Resolution:

    `msg_write` is not gated by `fifo_wready`.

I've tested hmac_back_pressure test with modified design. It still
fails. But the failure isn't due to the modified design but the
scoreboard assumes getting the fifo_full status which cannot be happen
as the request was back-pressured and accepted after fifo_full condition
is resolved.

Also, fifo_full interrupt now happens when MSG_FIFO and prim_packer both
cannot accept the new request, not only seeing MSG_FIFO `fifo_wready`.

Cindy has a fix PR for this issue.

[prim/packer] Revert the design prior to #634

Problem:

    `prim_packer` sent out partial data (mask_o != '1) in some case
    without `flush_i`.

While testing the `hmac_back_pressure`, the test failed at the assertion
below in `sha2_pad.sv`.

```systemverilog
  // When fifo_partial, fifo shouldn't be empty and hash_process was set
  `ASSERT(ValidPartialConditionAssert,
          fifo_partial && fifo_rvalid |-> hash_process_flag,
          clk_i, !rst_ni)
```

It complains when it receives not full word data from MSG_FIFO wihout
`hash_process` indication from the software. It means, something wrong
happens along the data path from TL-UL interface to sha2_pad logic.

The mask (which creates `fifo_partial`) is generated in `prim_packer`.
While reviewing the logic again, I found that the PR #634 I assumed
`prim_packer` has 64 bit internal registers (InW := 32 and OutW := 32).

But, when I designed it, I made it to have `max(InW, OutW)`, so if the
stored data + incoming data size exceeds `MaxW`, the logic should lower
`ready_o`. It worked well before changing the design.

While adding FPV assertions internally, I've assumed it wrong and
changed the design to store the incoming data if current stored data
size is less than or equal to `OutW`.

Resolution:

    Rolled-back the `prim_packer` to original and increased `pos_next`
    size to accomodate `InW + OutW` value, which is `Width + 1`.

This is related to #19

[prim/packer] Add more assertions for solid FPV

resolved_issues.body: Mainly to @eunchan  for creating the testcase (or at least covergroup) for `prim_packer` module.

resolved_issues.title: [prim/packer] Enhance the behavior based on FPV result
resolved_issues.body:
Problem 1:

    `prim_packer` did not assert `valid_o` even it has enough data to
    send out on some corner case when `ready_i` is de-asserted.

Lost the previous commit message. So let it be short. `prim_packer` is
a primitive module to pack incoming data with mask into `OutW` bit-width
signal and send out to the output port.

While preparing FPV environment, a new assertion was added:

    // If input mask is greater than output width, valid should be
    // asserted
    `ASSERT(ValidOAssertedForInputGTEOutW_A,
            valid_i && ($countones(mask_i) >= OutW) |-> valid_o,
            clk_i, !rst_ni)

FPV catches a corner case based on this assertion. When the output port
lowered `ready_i`, the module stores incoming request into the internal
registers. Then it increases `pos` pointer value by `InW`. At the next
cycle, it is expected to keep asserting the `valid_o` as it has data to
send out. As `pos_next` is wrapped around in next cycle if there is more
incoming data, the `valid_next` is lowered.

Resolution:

    Now `prim_packer` considers `pos` value to assert `valid_o` prior to
    compare `pos_next`.

Problem 2:

    `ready_o` falsely asserted as `pos_next` wrapped around.

This issue is similar with the Problem 1. Problem 1 didn't cause any
functionally incorrect behavior. This problem causes an issue. As it let
the design latch the data even doesn't have sufficient storage inside.

Resolution:

    `ready_next` logic doesn't look `pos_next` but only looks at `pos`.
    If `pos` is less than `OutW`, it has enough internal storage to
    store incoming packet. Also, remind that if output port acked the
    outgoing data, it can always store incoming data.

This is related to #19

#!/bin/bash
set -e

# Stage 1: checkout base_sha in a clean workspace (+submodules)
cd /home/opentitan
git reset --hard
git clean -fdx
git checkout 0f9bcddbb40fc91d133c960019806f8ae5b82b8c
git submodule update --init --recursive

# Stage 2: install repository apt dependencies (if present)
export DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive
if [[ -f apt-requirements.txt ]]; then
  echo "[INFO] Installing apt dependencies from apt-requirements.txt"
  cp apt-requirements.txt /tmp/opentitan-apt-requirements.txt
  sed -i -e '/^$/d' -e '/^#/d' -e 's/#.*//' /tmp/opentitan-apt-requirements.txt
  if [[ -s /tmp/opentitan-apt-requirements.txt ]]; then
    apt-get update
    xargs -r apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends < /tmp/opentitan-apt-requirements.txt
    rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
  else
    echo "[INFO] apt-requirements.txt is empty after filtering comments"
  fi
  rm -f /tmp/opentitan-apt-requirements.txt
else
  echo "[WARN] apt-requirements.txt not found at 0f9bcddbb40fc91d133c960019806f8ae5b82b8c; skipping repo-specific apt install"
fi

# Stage 3: install project-specific Python dependencies from the checked-out repo.
# This commit references the removed ipyxact master branch, so rewrite it to main.
# The standalone VCS reproducer does not use FuseSoC, so drop that line to avoid
# a slow modern dependency resolution path against the legacy edalize pin.
if [[ -f python-requirements.txt ]]; then
  echo "[INFO] Installing Python deps from python-requirements.txt"
  python -m pip install -U pip "setuptools<66.0.0"
  cp python-requirements.txt /tmp/opentitan-python-requirements.txt
  python - <<'PY'
from pathlib import Path
import re

path = Path("/tmp/opentitan-python-requirements.txt")
lines = []
for line in path.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines():
    stripped = line.strip()
    if stripped in {
        "types-dataclasses",
        "types-pkg_resources",
    }:
        continue
    line = line.replace(
        "git+https://github.com/olofk/ipyxact.git@master",
        "git+https://github.com/olofk/ipyxact.git@main",
    )
    if stripped == "fusesoc":
        continue
    line = re.sub(r'(#egg=[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+)\s+[<>=!~].*', r'\1', line)
    lines.append(line)
path.write_text("\n".join(lines) + "\n", encoding="utf-8")
PY
  python -m pip install -r /tmp/opentitan-python-requirements.txt --no-warn-script-location
  rm -f /tmp/opentitan-python-requirements.txt
else
  echo "[ERROR] python-requirements.txt not found at 0f9bcddbb40fc91d133c960019806f8ae5b82b8c"
  exit 1
fi

# Stage 4: install RISC-V toolchain + Verible, then persist their PATH.
# Use --force to avoid an interactive prompt when the container already has a different toolchain.
if [[ -f util/get-toolchain.py ]]; then
  toolchain_version=""
  if [[ -f util/container/Dockerfile ]]; then
    toolchain_version="$(sed -n 's/^ARG RISCV_TOOLCHAIN_TAR_VERSION=//p' util/container/Dockerfile | head -n1)"
  fi

  echo "[INFO] Installing RISC-V toolchain via util/get-toolchain.py"
  if [[ -n "$toolchain_version" ]]; then
    python util/get-toolchain.py --update --force -r "$toolchain_version"
  else
    echo "[WARN] RISCV_TOOLCHAIN_TAR_VERSION not found; falling back to util/get-toolchain.py defaults"
    python util/get-toolchain.py --update --force
  fi
else
  echo "[WARN] util/get-toolchain.py not found at 0f9bcddbb40fc91d133c960019806f8ae5b82b8c; skipping RISC-V toolchain install"
fi

verible_version=""
if [[ -f hw/tool_requirements.py ]]; then
  verible_version="$(python - <<'PY'
from pathlib import Path

ns = {}
exec(Path("hw/tool_requirements.py").read_text(encoding="utf-8"), ns)
reqs = ns.get("__TOOL_REQUIREMENTS__", {})
entry = reqs.get("verible", "")
if isinstance(entry, dict):
    print(entry.get("min_version", ""))
elif isinstance(entry, str):
    print(entry)
PY
)"
fi
if [[ -z "$verible_version" && -f util/container/Dockerfile ]]; then
  verible_version="$(sed -n 's/^ARG VERIBLE_VERSION=//p' util/container/Dockerfile | head -n1)"
fi

if [[ -n "$verible_version" ]]; then
  echo "[INFO] Installing Verible ${verible_version}"
  rm -rf /tools/verible
  mkdir -p /tools/verible
  curl -f -Ls -o /tmp/verible.tar.gz \
    "https://github.com/chipsalliance/verible/releases/download/${verible_version}/verible-${verible_version}-linux-static-x86_64.tar.gz"
  tar -C /tools/verible -xf /tmp/verible.tar.gz --strip-components=1

problem_statement:
## Description
`prim_packer` is the OpenTitan primitive that packs masked input data into fixed-width output words of configured width `OutW`. Under output back-pressure, it mishandles the case where the module already holds a partial word and a new masked input contributes enough additional valid bits to complete at least one full output word. In that situation, the module can expose an inconsistent handshake state even though a complete output word is pending.

## Expected Behavior
Once the buffered data covers one full `OutW`-wide output word, `prim_packer` must present that word as pending output: `valid_o` must remain asserted, the output must represent a full-width word rather than a partial one, and `ready_o` must deassert while the downstream interface keeps `ready_i` low and the pending word has not yet been accepted. When the downstream side later reasserts `ready_i`, the pending word may be transferred and the packer may accept new input again.

## Actual Behavior
If the downstream side is stalled and the buffered occupancy crosses the `OutW` boundary because of a new masked input, `prim_packer` may drop `valid_o` or keep `ready_o` asserted even though it has already accumulated a full output word and cannot safely store another input beat. This makes the module appear ready for more input while a complete output word is still waiting at the output.

## Trigger Condition
The bug is triggered when `prim_packer` has buffered a partial word, `ready_i` is low, and the next accepted input has enough asserted mask bits to make the total buffered data reach or exceed one full output word. One concrete example is a partial masked write followed by a full-width masked write while the output remains blocked.

problem_statement:
## Description
The affected logic is the OpenTitan Key Manager (`keymgr`) KMAC (Keccak Message Authentication Code) command-selection path. `Advance`, `Generate ID`, and `Generate Output` operations are driven by internal command-enable signals that are expected to be mutually exclusive; if multiple enables are asserted together, keymgr must treat that as an invalid command fault.

## Expected Behavior
A multi-hot command-enable fault must be latched as soon as it occurs, even if it lasts for only a single clock cycle while a KMAC-backed operation is already in progress. Once such a fault occurs, keymgr must report a fatal fault alert and enter its terminal `StDisabled` state rather than completing the operation normally.

## Actual Behavior
The invalid-command check is only combinational. If the command-enable signals become multi-hot briefly in the middle of a KMAC-backed operation and return to a legal value before the KMAC transaction finishes, the fault is lost. In that case keymgr does not report the fatal fault and can remain operational instead of transitioning to `StDisabled`.

## Trigger Condition
This occurs when a transient hardware fault or glitch makes more than one internal keymgr KMAC command enable active at the same time during an in-flight KMAC-backed command. A concrete affected scenario is an `Advance` command issued after keymgr has already reached the Initialized (`StInit`) working state, followed by a one-cycle multi-hot condition on the internal command enables before the KMAC operation completes.

problem_statement:
The OpenTitan Key Manager IP contains a hardware-input validation block that checks several hardware-supplied values before they are accepted. One of those values is the health-state input, which is 128 bits wide. In the current implementation, supplying an all-ones health-state value is incorrectly accepted because the check is performed using a wider 256-bit comparison width, so the narrower value is effectively treated as zero-extended during the invalid-value check.

Expected behavior: the health-state input must be validated at its native 128-bit width. When the health-state input is all ones at that width, it must be rejected as invalid, and the corresponding health-state valid indication must deassert.

Affected module: the Key Manager IP's hardware input validation logic, specifically the `keymgr_input_checks` path that validates the health-state input.

Trigger condition: this occurs when the Key Manager validates `health_state_i` and that input is driven to an all-ones 128-bit value while the other hardware inputs are otherwise valid.

resolved_issues.body:
Hey Michael, 
I have three questions/issues related to OTP_CHECK failure.

1. If otp check has timeout error, it reports incorrect status error:
   Expected status: "timeout_error" should stay high;
   Actual status: "timeout_error" is high for ONE CLOCK CYCLE, then "lsfr_fsm_error" stays high.
   
   Reason: [`chk_timeout_d`](https://github.com/lowRISC/opentitan/blob/master/hw/ip/otp_ctrl/rtl/otp_ctrl_lfsr_timer.sv#L211) is cleared when state machine changes from `IntegWaitSt` to `ErrorSt`.
Please refer to the screenshot below:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/11466553/110259794-64385980-7f5e-11eb-9ca8-9167eb036803.png)

2. Regarding `check_pending` status, I found the `check_pending` status will stay high even if any check failure are found.
   
   For example if we have a ECC uncorrectable error.  A fatal alert will trigger, but LFSR state machine will be stuck at ["CnstyWaitSt"](https://github.com/lowRISC/opentitan/blob/master/hw/ip/otp_ctrl/rtl/otp_ctrl_lfsr_timer.sv#L265) state, and status `check_pending` field will be `1` until reset or timeout.
This is because in `otp_ctrl_part_buf.sv` we only return [`integ_chk_ack_o = 1'b1`](https://github.com/lowRISC/opentitan/blob/master/hw/ip/otp_ctrl/rtl/otp_ctrl_part_buf.sv#L332) if a check is passed. 
I want to double check if the behavior is expected? Would it be more clear if design exits `CnstyWaitSt` state and clear `check_pending` bit after ECC uncorrectable error is found.

3. In [otp_ctrl spec](https://docs.opentitan.org/hw/ip/otp_ctrl/doc/index.html#partition-checks) I found a statement saying: "If a failure is encountered, the OTP controller will send out a fatal_check_error alert and reset all of its hardware outputs to their defaults."
  Are the "defaults value" referring to the values before OTP_INIT or after OTP_INIT?

Thanks for your time and inputs :)
Cindy

problem_statement:
## Description
The bug is in the OpenTitan OTP (One-Time Programmable) controller's response to a fatal check error. The controller contains multiple partition controllers and internal finite state machines (FSMs) that keep buffered partition data on hardware-facing outputs. When one partition check or internal OTP FSM detects a fatal condition, the design raises a fatal alert, but the fatal condition is not propagated across the rest of the controller.

## Affected Function
The affected functionality is the OTP controller's block-wide fatal-error handling across partition controllers and internal FSMs, especially the invalidation of buffered hardware outputs derived from OTP partitions.

## Expected Behavior
If a background OTP partition check fails and raises `fatal_check_error`, the OTP controller should force all relevant partition controllers and internal FSMs into their terminal error state as part of its local fatal-error response. Buffered hardware outputs that expose partition contents should then stop reporting valid data and return to their RTL-default invalid state, rather than remaining valid until some later external escalation occurs.

## Actual Behavior
A background check failure can raise `fatal_check_error` while only the faulting FSM moves to its terminal error state. Other partition controllers can keep running, and buffered outputs carrying OTP-derived hardware configuration or life cycle data can remain valid even though the fatal alert has already been raised.

## Trigger Condition
This occurs when a background OTP check fails in one partition or internal FSM before any external escalation arrives. A representative case is a check timeout: the controller raises `fatal_check_error`, but not all buffered hardware outputs are invalidated.

problem_statement:
## Description
The OpenTitan AON (always-on) timer IP contains a wakeup timer that is expected to keep running from the always-on clock while the rest of the chip is in low-power mode. In the observed failure, after the wakeup timer is programmed and low-power mode is entered, the wakeup timer stops advancing even though the life cycle controller escalation signal is inactive. Because the count stalls, the programmed wakeup threshold is never reached and the wakeup expiration interrupt does not fire.

## Expected Behavior
If the wakeup timer is enabled and the life cycle controller escalation signal is inactive, entering low-power mode must not pause the wakeup timer. After software programs the threshold and enables the timer, the prescaler and wakeup counter must continue incrementing on the always-on clock during sleep, and the wakeup expiration interrupt must assert when the counter reaches the programmed threshold.

## Actual Behavior
In low-power mode with the life cycle controller escalation signal inactive, the wakeup timer's counting path is blocked and the wakeup counter stops increasing. As a result, the wakeup timer does not expire and its interrupt is not generated.

## Affected Function
AON (always-on) timer IP, specifically the wakeup timer counting and expiry logic in the always-on clock domain.

## Trigger Condition
Program a wakeup threshold, enable the wakeup timer, and then enter low-power mode while the life cycle controller escalation signal remains inactive. Under this condition, the wakeup timer should continue running, but it stalls instead.

title: [rom_ctrl] Fix gnt/rvalid timing just after initial check finishes
body:
The `rom_ctrl` block is supposed to give access just to the checker
until the checker is finished, at which point the bus can start
accessing data.

To control this, there is a mux with a `sel_i` signal. When `sel_i` is 1,
the checker is still running. When it drops to zero (a one-time
event), the bus should have access.

Before this patch, there was a bug where the block would seemingly
respond to a request in zero time, raising the bus grant signal and
`rvalid` at the same time. The problem was just that we were incorrectly
using a registered signal for the grant: the ROM had taken the request
a cycle earlier but we didn't tell the bus.

Fixes #6516.

[rom_ctrl] Fix gnt/rvalid timing just after initial check finishes

The rom_ctrl block is supposed to give access just to the checker
until the checker is finished, at which point the bus can start

To control this, there is a mux with a sel_i signal. When sel_i is 1,
the checker is still running. When it drops to zero (a one-time
event), the bus should have access.

Before this patch, there was a bug where the block would seemingly
respond to a request in zero time, raising the bus grant signal and
rvalid at the same time. The problem was just that we were incorrectly
using a registered signal for the grant: the ROM had taken the request
a cycle earlier but we didn't tell the bus.

resolved_issues.title: [rom_ctrl] Bus grant does not match bus req
resolved_issues.body:
There really are two issues here. 

Background: This was uncovered when running the pwrmgr smoketest in DV. The test configures AON to wake up at a point where pwrmgr has transitioned to low power state. Following that, the pwrmgr brings resources out of reset. That is when the following assertion gets thrown:

```console
"../src/lowrisc_tlul_adapter_sram_0.1/rtl/tlul_adapter_sram.sv", 458: tb.dut.top_earlgrey.u_rom_ctrl.u_tl_adapte
r_rom.rvalidHighReqFifoEmpty: started at 1366300000ps failed at 1366300000ps
        Offending 'reqfifo_rvalid'
UVM_ERROR @ 1366300000 ps: (tlul_adapter_sram.sv:458) [ASSERT FAILED] rvalidHighReqFifoEmpty
```

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/46467186/118060426-a22f7080-b347-11eb-9929-ea26e257482b.png)


It appears that the `rom_ctrl_mux`, upon reset, has to contend with both, the checker req (which is given preference) and the bus req. The `rom_req_o` stays asserted as the req transitions from the checker req and the bus req (and hence so does the `rom_rvalid_i`, response from the ROM). 


Investigating it further (with @eunchan and @msfschaffner's help), the `rom_req_o` logic seemed strange:
https://github.com/lowRISC/opentitan/blob/2f033140747084d07f2530b3b6471a4a20d18679/hw/ip/rom_ctrl/rtl/rom_ctrl_mux.sv#L63

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/46467186/118075031-1710a380-b364-11eb-8048-6d29b19a6fb9.png)

It also seemed strange to see that signal stay asserted while `rst_ni` is active. 

The following fix seems to have worked - it got the test to pass:
```systemverilog
    assign rom_req_o  = sel_q ? sel_i      : bus_req_i;
```

A better approach may be to implement an FSM that does the switch between ROM checker and bus access.

problem_statement:
## Description
The OpenTitan ROM controller IP (`rom_ctrl`) uses `rom_ctrl_mux` to hand over ROM access from the internal ROM checker to the system bus. While `sel_i` is 1, the checker owns the ROM port. When the initial ROM check finishes, `sel_i` transitions to 0 and the bus is allowed to start issuing ROM reads.

## Affected Function
The affected logic is the `rom_ctrl_mux` handover from checker-owned ROM access to bus-owned ROM access, specifically the timing relationship between `bus_gnt_o` and `bus_rvalid_o` for the first bus transaction after the initial check completes.

## Trigger Condition
The failure occurs when checker traffic has been active, `sel_i` changes from 1 to 0, and the bus issues its first ROM request in that same cycle. This can happen immediately after reset release or wake-up, when the initial ROM check has just completed and the bus starts reading ROM right away.

## Expected Behavior
If the first bus ROM request is asserted in the same cycle that `sel_i` drops from 1 to 0, that request must be granted in that cycle. The corresponding `bus_rvalid_o` must only assert on a later cycle as the response to that granted bus request. The checker-to-bus handover must not make the transfer appear to complete in zero time.

## Actual Behavior
At the checker-to-bus handover, `rom_ctrl_mux` can assert `bus_rvalid_o` for the first bus access even though the bus request was not granted in the previous cycle. In practice, the first post-check bus transaction can appear to receive `bus_gnt_o` and `bus_rvalid_o` together, which makes the response look zero-latency and violates the bus-facing request/response contract.

resolved_issues.title: [keymgr] LC turns off when advancing from StReset to StInit
resolved_issues.body:
@tjaychen 
advancing from StReset to StInit is a bit special. When LC turns off during this operation, op_status will be success and no error, no alert will be triggered. State is updated to StInvalid and key are wiped. Does this make sense? Triggering an error seems better.

![Screen Shot 2021-04-02 at 11 34 03 AM](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/49293026/113443703-58965200-93a7-11eb-93e3-8dbd35b26f5c.png)

wave:
/edascratch/weicai-opentitan/ot/km_regr/keymgr-sim-vcs/9.keymgr_lc_disable/out

problem_statement:
## Description
The OpenTitan key manager (`keymgr`) control finite-state machine mishandles an in-flight `OpAdvance` operation that performs the initial transition from `StReset` to `StInit`. If the life cycle controller disables the key manager by deasserting the key manager enable signal (`keymgr_en`) before that initial advance has finished, the block can abandon initialization and enter an invalid state while still reporting the advance as successful.

## Expected Behavior
If `keymgr_en` drops while the `StReset` to `StInit` advance is still in progress, that advance must be marked as an error, not as a successful completion. In this situation, the key manager may move to `StInvalid` and wipe key material because it has been disabled, but software-visible `OP_STATUS` must report that the in-flight operation failed.

## Actual Behavior
When `keymgr_en` is deasserted during an in-progress `StReset` to `StInit` advance, the key manager updates its state to `StInvalid` and wipes keys, yet `OP_STATUS` can still report success and no operation error is recorded.

## Trigger Condition
Start an `OpAdvance` from `StReset`, then disable the key manager before the transition reaches `StInit`. The bug is specific to the initial reset-to-init advance while that operation is still in flight.

title: Spi stall fix2
body:
- Reverts changes to core state variables made in #7377
    - No more "actual" or "prestall" state
    
- Still correctly solves errors noted in #7281 with the following changes:
    - Adds signal command_ready_int to internally track non-stall-condition values for command_ready_o
    - Internal signal new_command now depends on command_ready_int, not command_ready_o
    - command_ready_o is masked to always output 0 during a stall condition.
    - All registers and output signals are now enabled only when !stall
    - The name of the state register has been renamed to simply "state_d/q"
    
- This results in a far simpler scheme for managing the FSM, with fewer coverage points to worry about.  The previous version, though functional, left some uncertainty as to how to establish coverage points for the "actual" and "prestall" states.
    
- Removes corresponding TODOs from the documentation
    
Signed-off-by: Martin Lueker-Boden <martin.lueker-boden@wdc.com>

**Note to Reviewers:** In order to make the review easier this PR is currently organized into three commits:
1. Reversion of #7377 (unchanged, no real need to review)
2. Renaming `spi_host_st_d/spi_host_st_q` to `state_d/state_q`
3. Actual alternative bug fixes to handle #7281 in a more simple fashion

commits.message:
[ spi_host, rtl ] Simplify SPI_HOST FSM stall behavior

- Reverts changes to core state variables made in #7377
    - No more "actual" or "prestall" state

Still correctly solves errors noted in #7281 with the following changes:
- Adds signal command_ready_int to internally track non-stall-condition values
  for command_ready_o
- Internal signal new_command now depends on command_ready_int, not command_ready_o
- command_ready_o is masked to always output 0 during a stall condition.
- All registers and output signals are now enabled only when !stall
- The name of the state register has been renamed to simply "state_d/q"

This results in a far simpler scheme for managing the FSM, with fewer coverage points
to worry about.  The previous version, though functional, left some uncertainty as
to how to establish coverage points for the "actual" and "prestall" states.

- Removes corresponding TODOs from the documentation

Signed-off-by: Martin Lueker-Boden <martin.lueker-boden@wdc.com>

resolved_issues.title: [spi_host,design] Properly handle TX "stall" and "flush" conditions
resolved_issues.body:
This commit handles two FSM bugs in the SPI_HOST TX path.

1. This commit adds a separate "prestall" copy of the FSM state to
prevent commands being dropped when no data is avaiable in the TX queue.
Since a stall prevents the FSM from updating command_valid signals were
previously being ignored during stall conditions, as the state machine
would not transition at this time.   This is solved by queuing an update
of the FSM in the "prestall" state variable, and performing the state
transition once the stall has been resolved.
NOTE: the simpler solution of deasserting command_ready during stalls does
not work, because the stall condition depends on the state, which in turn
depends on command_ready.  Making the FSM state directly dependent on
stall creates an unresolvable logical cycle.

2. Previous to this commit, the FSM cmd_end signal was being sent at the very
beginning of each segment (when byte_cntr_q was zero).  This was causing
the byte select to imcorrectly flush any additional words from the first
data word. This is fixed here by triggering cmd_end_o when byte_cntr_q == 1,
just as we are loading the segment's last byte into the shift register.

Fixes #7281, Fixes #7621

Signed-off-by: Martin Lueker-Boden <martin.lueker-boden@wdc.com>

problem_statement:
## Description
OpenTitan's SPI_HOST (Serial Peripheral Interface host controller) mishandles write-command handshaking when the transmit (TX) path stalls at the start of a segment. If software submits a write segment and the transmit side cannot supply the first byte, the SPI_HOST finite-state machine enters a TX stall but can still expose its internal command handshake as ready.

## Expected Behavior
When a write segment is stalled waiting for transmit data, the command must remain pending and SPI_HOST must apply backpressure until the stall is resolved. In particular, while the transmit-stall output (`tx_stall_o`) is asserted for that write command, the internal command-ready output (`command_ready_o`) must stay low so the command is not treated as accepted during the stall.

## Actual Behavior
A write command can encounter a transmit stall and still see the internal command-ready handshake behave as though the SPI_HOST FSM is ready. That allows the command to be treated as accepted even though the write segment has not started making forward progress, which can leave a basic SPI write transaction stuck without beginning on the bus.

## Affected Function
The affected block is the SPI_HOST transmit-side finite-state machine, specifically the logic that combines TX-stall detection with the command ready/accept handshake for write segments.

## Trigger Condition
The failure occurs when SPI_HOST receives a write-enabled command at the same time the transmit path cannot provide the first byte of the segment, causing a TX stall immediately as the command reaches the FSM.

problem_statement:
## Description
The OpenTitan SPI_HOST IP can drop transmitted data in segmented standard-mode write transactions when software queues consecutive segments and uses `CSAAT` (chip-select active after transfer) to keep chip-select asserted across segment boundaries.

## Affected Function
This affects the SPI_HOST finite-state machine and transmit segment-completion logic that determine when a write segment is finished and when the active-low chip-select signal (`CSB`) may be deasserted between segments.

## Expected Behavior
In a multi-segment SPI_HOST write transaction, each segment must transmit exactly its configured number of bytes before the controller advances to the next segment. If a non-final segment has `CSAAT=1`, `CSB` must remain asserted while the next segment starts, and `CSB` may deassert only after the final segment with `CSAAT=0` completes. For a three-segment transfer programmed for 1 byte, then 4 bytes, then 2 bytes, the SPI bus must emit all 7 bytes in order, and `CSB` must rise only once after the seventh byte.

## Actual Behavior
The controller can treat a segmented write transfer as complete one byte too early when handing off between back-to-back segments. In the failing pattern, the first 1-byte segment is transmitted, but the following 4-byte segment loses its fourth byte, so only 6 total bytes are sent before `CSB` is released.

## Trigger Condition
The bug is triggered by back-to-back SPI_HOST standard-mode write segments where a non-final segment sets `CSAAT=1` to keep `CSB` low across the boundary, and a later segment clears `CSAAT`. A concrete failing case is a 1-byte segment followed by a 4-byte segment and then a 2-byte segment.

resolved_issues.body:
It appears that np_sample_cnt_q[15:0] is not being reset when the set of matching filters changes as required by the design spec.

> All pairs of filters that are enabled in adc_chn0_filter_ctl[7:0] and adc_chn1_filter_ctl[7:0] are evaluated after each pair of samples has been taken. The filter result is passed to the periodic scan counter if enabled and not at its limit otherwise the result is passed to the debounce counter. The list below describes how the counters interpret the filter results:
If no filters are hit then the counter will reset to zero.
**If one or more filters are hit but the set hit differs from the previous evaluation the counter resets to zero.**
If one or more filters are hit and either none was hit in the previous evaluation or the same set was hit in the previous evaluation and the counter is not at its limit then the counter will increment.

To reproduce:
gh pr checkout 10147
./util/dvsim/dvsim.py hw/ip/adc_ctrl/dv/adc_ctrl_sim_cfg.hjson -i adc_ctrl_filters_polled --fixed-seed 1 --tool xcelium --waves

problem_statement:
## Description
The OpenTitan ADC (Analog-to-Digital Converter) controller IP (`adc_ctrl`) does not follow the design-spec semantics of the normal-power (NP) debounce counter (`np_sample_cnt`) when the set of matching enabled filter pairs changes. After each pair of channel samples is evaluated, if the current non-zero filter-match bitmap differs from the previous non-zero filter-match bitmap, the NP debounce sequence must restart for the new bitmap instead of reusing debounce history from the old one.

## Expected Behavior
A debounce-complete result must be reported only after `np_sample_cnt` consecutive evaluations of the same non-zero filter-match bitmap. If the match bitmap changes to a different non-zero value, the accumulated NP debounce count must be cleared and the new bitmap must start a fresh debounce run. This rule also applies when the controller has just moved from low-power (LP) periodic scanning into continuous NP scanning.

## Actual Behavior
When the controller is already accumulating NP debounce history, a later evaluation with a different non-zero filter-match bitmap can inherit the previous count. In that case the ADC controller can report debounce completion too early for the new filter match.

## Trigger Condition
The failure occurs when one filter-match bitmap has already contributed to NP debouncing and a later evaluation produces a different non-zero bitmap before the new bitmap has been debounced for the full configured NP sample count. One concrete failing case is the LP-to-NP path: an LP periodic scan sees one matching filter set, NP scanning begins, and then the match bitmap changes to a different non-zero filter set.
